speechtext:
Order. It is evident that a number of announcements are required to be made at the resumption of this session. Some special proceedings have been discussed and possibly will be agreed to; all of which will take some time. We should address our attention, I think, after the expiry of these rather special announcements to the preservation of an appropriate question period which, pursuant to the special order under which we continue to operate, would expire at three o'clock. Obviously, that would deprive members of their right to ask questions, particularly on this of all days. Therefore, I suggest that we take at a proper pace the rather special proceedings that may intervene between now and the commencement of the question period, and seek at that time a consensus whether we should safeguard 40 or 45 minutes for questions at that time.
May I begin by calling to the attention of the House two resignations which I have received in due form from former hon. members. The first is from the Hon. Gerard Pelletier, the former member for the electoral district of Hochelaga. The second is from Mr. Walter Carter, the former hon. member for St. John's West. Both resignations have been received in due form and are in order.

speakeroldname: Mr. Speaker:
speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Hon. members will notice, for the first time, probably, in the experience if not of all hon. members of the House, then of one or two, the absence from the table of Mr. Gordon Dubroy. Mr. Dubroy has been Clerk Assistant to this House and has served in other capacities with a quality that is so extraordinary as to escape adequate description by me. The fact that he is not here is the result of his retirement last spring. When I was first elected to this position he was ready then to retire, but I begged him to stay on because I valued his counsel and advice. Experience has taught me that persuading him to stay was one of the most important and salutary moves I ever could have made.
Mr. Dubroy finally prevailed upon us, in the summer, to accept his resignation and it was time for his retirement to begin. I wish all hon. members to know that I invited Mr. Dubroy to be here today at the table in order to hear not only my tribute but, I am sure, the tributes that will be expressed to him by representatives of all parties in the House. His absence from the House is certainly not due to his unwillingness to accept my invitation but, unfortunately, because he is at present in hospital in Ottawa, where this morning he underwent rather serious surgery. We are awaiting reports from the hospital but, regretfully, I cannot be optimistic at this time. When further news is available, I will certainly pass it along to hon. members.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Speaker:
speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We find ourselves blessed with the replacement for Mr. Dubroy in the person of Mr. Charles Beverley Koester, the former Clerk of the legislature of Saskatchewan. The Privy Council has blessed us with a man of experience and skill.
I would not want to undertake to describe the qualifications that would be required to fill the post that has been left vacant by Mr. Dubroy, but certainly it is our early indication that Mr. Koester possesses all of those qualifications. I know all hon. members would want to wish him well in that distinguished position.
Hear, hear!

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with your indulgence, and before we begin to discuss matters which might reveal some slight differences of opinion among hon. members, I want to draw attention to a remarkable anniversary of a remarkable man, a man whose character and achievements elicit unanimous respect and universal admiration. It was on October 14, 1935-40 years ago today-that the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) was first elected to this House.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Trudeau:
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: It is astonishing to realize that a man so young in spirit and a man whose ideas and priorities are so relevant to today and tomorrow took his seat in this House before any of the rest of us were here and before many of the rest of us were born.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: Not you.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakeroldname: Mr. Trudeau:
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
It is even more astonishing to realize that a man of such phenomenal energy will have 71 candles on the cake when he celebrates his birthday next Monday.

The respect which the hon. member enjoys in the House is not only ascribable to his vitality, his age, but is especially due to his distinguished contribution to federal politics and to the valuable services which he has rendered and which he continues to render to his country.
Throughout his long career as churchman, Member of Parliament, premier of Saskatchewan during 17 years and leader of the New Democratic Party, he has worked with untiring eagerness to see Canada achieve the objectives which he had set for himself on reaching adulthood, namely independence and national unity, civil liberties and equality of opportunities and above all social justice.

Over the years he has known moments of triumph, but never of despair; he has heard criticisms of his policies, but never of his integrity. His experience of the hunger, poverty and unemployment of the depression years on the prairies has left a permanent mark on his soul and has made him a lifelong man of the people. He has pleaded the cause of the common man from one end of Canada to the other, and left behind in each community he has visited a lasting impression of warmth, compassion, wit and tireless energy. All of us in this House know him as a skilful and formidable speaker, a man who always keeps his word, a man who is willing to forget sharp words spoken in the
October 14, 1975

heat of debate even though he seems incapable of forgetting any fact he ever learned.
In the name of everyone on this side of the House, I want to salute a man whose presence here continues to earn for parliament the respect of Canadians everywhere.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)-at least for this occasion today-on behalf of myself and my party in paying tribute to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas).
I think the first thing that should be noticed about the hon. gentleman and his life is that he was an immigrant. I do not know just what effect this is going to have upon the attitudes of various people in Canada toward future immigration policy. The second thing is that I understand he was an amateur boxing champion, which no doubt explains why he is so familiar with Murphy's law. I understand that an antagonistic voter once tried to ridicule the hon. gentleman by saying that Mr. Douglas was so small he could eat him, and the hon. gentleman replied, "If you ate me, you would have more brains in your stomach than in your head."

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: As the Prime Minister has outlined, his public career has been very long, very honourable and very distinguished. I have known him for quite a long time. I knew him first when he was premier of the province of Saskatchewan and I was premier of an even greater province.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: The hon. gentleman and I have not always agreed, but I want to say that he exemplifies an extraordinarily rare combination of generosity, of spirit, of good humour, of tenacity and courage, not to mention eloquence. He has given a great deal to this parliament, to the legislature of Saskatchewan and to our country. I respect him; I like him. I congratulate him for his record of years of public service. Personally, and on behalf of my party colleagues, I wish him many years of health, happiness and continued controversy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Real Caouette (Temiscamingue):
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I wish to join the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in extending our wishes to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas). The hon. member was for many years the premier of Saskatchewan. Indeed, he led the CCF party to power in that province, thus forming the first CCF government in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister referred to October 1935. That year, William Aberhart was elected under the banner of Social Credit. A few months later, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands was a federal candidate in Saskatchewan. The member was then well known in the west. He was therefore elected in 1935. I was told that he used to drive a 1933 or 1934 car on which could be read on one side: Vote CCF and on the other: Vote Social Credit. He was therefore the real representative of two political parties when he was elected for the first time
Mr. T. C. Douglas
in 1935. And at that time he so attracted the attention of the people-it is to be noted-that he even attracted not only the sympathy and friendship, but also the conviction of the present Prime Minister. At that time, the Prime Minister was strongly in favour of the CCF party. Therefore, this means that the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) has commanded the respect of a number of people who shared his convictions.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to include the hon. member among my good friends. He is devoted and he has earned the sympathy not only of the members of his own political party, but also the sympathy of others who appreciate him as a man. For instance, in Ponteix, Saskatchewan, where all my relations on my maternal side have been living since 1909-all were authentic Liberals-when Tommy Douglas canvassed in an election in Saskatchewan, and became minister, we heard them say: We are not CCFers but we cannot vote against Tommy. That is how people voted for Tommy and that is how he attracted the sympathy and friendship of the whole population of his province and of Canada.
Therefore, I join with the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Official Opposition to wish him a happy anniversary next Monday. He is seventy-one and yet he does not look a day older than fifty. This means he is in perfect physical form. Once again, I wish him many more years during which he can continue to devote himself to the whole population. Obviously, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands is an asset for the House of Commons. He is a man who sets a good example and those who follow him in the field of work and courage are not going wrong. In the name of my colleagues and in my own name, I extend every good wish to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. May he continue to devote his time and energy for the good of all Canadians.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I through you express my sincere thanks to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), the leader of the Social Credit party, the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette), and my own leader, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), for the very nice things they have said and for their felicitations to me on this, the fortieth anniversary of my having been elected to the House of Commons. I must confess that I have been trying to suppress the fact that I came to this House five years before the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Die-fenbaker) and seven years before the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) because I did not want to destroy the common concept that these two distinguished members were here when the place started.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: I must confess that I am overwhelmed by the fulsome praise that has been lavished upon me by the leaders of the various political parties, and I want to say that I have had some difficulty in recognizing myself: I know many people across Canada will have even greater difficulty recognizing these descriptions of me. subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands):
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
On
October 14, 1935, I was elected to this chamber as a private member. Forty years later, I am still a private member. My only consolation is that I am holding my own.
When I entered public life, I tried to fix one principle in mind; that is, that I would never allow my political differences to interfere with my personal friendships. I can honestly say this afternoon that I have had friends, and some of them close personal friends, in all the political parties and that I have friends in all parts of this chamber. Therefore, I feel something like the old man who, when he was asked how it was that he did not have an enemy in the world, said, "It is very simple; I outlived the bastards."

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands):
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
It is
always the tendency for men and women, as they grow older, to glorify the past and to belittle the present. However, I can say with complete sincerity that while the House of Commons in the second half of the 1930s had in it

some political giants, I think the House of Commons today is more dynamic, more lively. We have a better committees' system. We have a better rapport with the constituencies, thanks to the constituency offices and sending out of household mail. I think there is now a better understanding between the people and the elected members than probably at any other time in my political experience.
I look back on four decades of public life, some 22 years in this House and almost 18 years in the legislature of Saskatchewan, and I am convinced more than ever in the effectiveness of parliamentary government. We may not always move as quickly as we should. We do not always advance as rapidly as I would like to see it done. I have never believed in the old cliche that government is the art of the possible. That is often the excuse for caution and timidity. I believe that government is the art of the impossible.
In 40 years I have seen new programs introduced; I have seen new government agencies set up; I have seen social and economic changes which 40 years ago would have been considered sheer madness.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands):

I would like to thank those who have spoken, and hon. members in all parts of the House, for their good wishes as I begin my second 40 years of public endeavour on behalf of the political principles to which I adhere.

Mr. Speaker, as my motion concerns more precisely the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), I should like to congratulate him for his appointment and wish him well for the welfare of Canada.
Pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I seek the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with a very important and urgent matter.
In view of the ever increasing interest rates being the main cause of inflation that affects mostly low wage earners and Parliament being the assembly of the people's delegates, who is the supreme authority in Canada, seconded by the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) I move:
That the House recommend to the government and the Minister of Finance to order the Bank of Canada to announce immediately a reduction of interest rates in order to check the voraciousness of credit controllers in the country and at the same time really control inflation.

My question arises out of the Prime Minister's address last night in which he made reference to the introduction of controls on prices and profits. Can he explain whether the government intends to introduce a price control mechanism distinct from the profit guidelines, or are prices to be controlled only by means of such guidelines which would only operate after the event, so to speak, and only if the board should decide to look into the books of a particular company?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I thank the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby for his kind remarks. As the hon. member might note from the white paper, the circumstances will very much depend on whether the cost increase in respect of a particular product can be clearly allocated to it, or whether the cost is so intermingled with others that one would have to follow another system. In the case of one in respect of which the cost can be allocated, then the only price increase that will be permissible will be one on which actual cost increase has been proven. With regard to unallocable costs, in some industries and, of course, with regard to the distribution sector, the question of profit margin would then be the basis for determination and application of the guidelines.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Solicitor General of Canada.
On a number of occasions I asked the Solicitor General whether the government would enforce the capital punishment legislation. He has always replied that he had other means to protect society. In the case of Mr. Martel who committed suicide the other day and killed a 6 year old child, the minister claimed that it had been through an administrative error that he had been out on seven or eight occasions. Recently, we had the case of a Mr. Clermont who was sentenced to hang some twenty years ago and who was out on five or six occasions. Could the minister tell us whether this was also due to an administrative error?

speakeroldname: Hon. Warren Allmand (Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF ADMINISTRATIVE ERROR IN PAROLING OF MR. MARTEL AND MR. CLERMONT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would have to check on the second case. In the first case of Martel, there was an unfortunate incident in that the warrant of arrest for Martel was delivered by court officials to the wrong prison, to Parthenais rather than the federal penitentiary. Mr. Martel was not, as some newspapers say, out of parole. As a matter of fact he was refused by the parole board both times he applied, but he was released at the end of sentence on mandatory supervision. He would have been kept in if the new warrant of arrest had been delivered to the right place. This is the administrative error to which reference was made. Since that time we have had a meeting in Montreal with the court officials, with the police, with the parole board and so on, and we are taking steps to make sure this sort of thing does not happen again. This is not all within my jurisdiction; some is municipal and some is provincial.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister and has to do with the meeting with the provincial premiers in connection with this problem of inflation. In view of the fact that many of the means whereby inflation can be controlled are within provincial jurisdiction, as he has said on more than one occasion, and in view of the fact that before the federal parliament can enact legislation which would be effective it would be necessary to have in the preamble of the statute or in a section set apart for the purpose a declaration that there was in effect a serious state of emergency, did the Prime Minister obtain the consent of all the premiers in respect of the insertion of such a term in the act so as to ensure that it will not be subject to successful attack in the Supreme Court of Canada.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-CONSENT OF PREMIERS TO DECLARATION OF EMERGENCY AS BASIS FOR LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can say the matter was discussed by the premiers. I did not ask them for, and did not obtain from them, any statement to the effect they would react immediately in a final way, and therefore I would not want to speak for their various positions which I hope will be made known as soon as possible; but the matter was discussed. The federal government is aware of the motion put forward by the right hon. gentleman. I would just add that I agree in part with the right hon. gentleman, but there are other headings under which the federal government does claim jurisdiction other than the peace, order and good government section alone. There is the commercial power and there is the banking power as well as many other powers exercised in the course of this legislation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Diefenbaker:
subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-CONSENT OF PREMIERS TO DECLARATION OF EMERGENCY AS BASIS FOR LEGISLATION
speechtext: All of that is correct in theory, but not in fact. The Supreme Court of Canada has made perfectly clear in a number of judgments that for the federal parliament to intrude in those areas within the jurisdiction of the provinces it would be necessary to have a declaration on the part of parliament that an emergency in fact existed. I suggest to him, and await his reply, that without such a term whatever legislation is introduced would be like conducting a war against inflation with pillows and platitudes.

speakeroldname: Mr. Trudeau:
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-CONSENT OF PREMIERS TO DECLARATION OF EMERGENCY AS BASIS FOR LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I might be able to reassure the right hon. gentleman by telling him at this stage I have no cause to believe the preamble, as it appears in the legislation, will be challenged as to its constitutionality by the premiers; but as the right hon. gentleman knows it is open to any Canadian to challenge the constitutionality of an act. We will have to see if the federal act is constitutional or not. We are convinced it is. I am just indicating to the right hon. gentleman that we are not invoking merely the grounds that he has suggested but are reserving the right to plead before the Supreme Court that many other aspects of federal jurisdiction are involved.

speakeroldname: Mr. Tom Cossitt (Leeds):
subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-ALLEGED TAPPING OF MEMBERS' TELEPHONES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a
question of privilege concerning a matter which I believe
will be of grave concern to members on all sides of the

October 14, 1975
Privilege-Mr. Cossitt
House. I refer to information which has come to me that indicates clearly and beyond a doubt that telephone calls being made by members of parliament and possibly, also, by public servants from various places in Canada to their offices here in Ottawa or to other government offices in Ottawa are being periodically listened to in a manner which I will now describe.
The calls to which I refer are those which are made over what are commonly referred to as incoming watts lines which are available for use by public servants and members of parliament to make calls to government offices in Ottawa including members' own offices. Since this system was installed I have made use of it, as I am sure other members have also done, and it first came to my attention on a number of occasions that at intervals of approximately 30 to 45 seconds I was hearing clicking noises-

subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-ALLEGED TAPPING OF MEMBERS' TELEPHONES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-ALLEGED TAPPING OF MEMBERS' TELEPHONES
speechtext: You hear that even when you are not on the phone.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cossitt:
subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-ALLEGED TAPPING OF MEMBERS' TELEPHONES
speechtext:
-that sounded as if someone was coming on the line at such points. I therefore made immediate inquiries with several operators involved on these occasions, and was advised by the operators that they had instructions to check at certain intervals for the purpose, so they said, of seeing if a line was still in use, by listening for conversation. I then asked to speak to the senior supervisor on duty, and would like to cite as an example the conversation that I had with Mrs. Breton who was the supervisor on duty when such an incident occurred on October 1.
Mrs. Breton confirmed information given to me by another supervisor on a previous date that operators were under instructions to check the lines at approximately 45-second intervals to determine if conversation was in progress. She further stated that the reason a check was being made for conversation was that Bell Telephone equipment was such that when both parties hung up, the operator did not receive a disconnection and therefore there was no way of knowing whether the call was completed, without making such frequent checks. Any excuse that the checking is done mechanically without actual listening on the line could scarcely be accurate since on at least four occasions I was able to speak directly to and question the operator who was, in effect, listening in.
I	find it difficult to accept the fact that Bell Canada's equipment is such that they do not know when a call is completed, and indeed I have since checked this point with persons in Bell Canada who tell me that they have no knowledge of equipment of this inadequate nature. I also asked who, specifically, had issued the instructions that telephone calls were to be monitored in this fashion and I was advised that any such instructions were never issued by Bell Canada and could presumably only have come from the Department of Communications of the Govern-

ment of Canada, and presumably specifically from or through the office of the man who I gather is in charge of government telecommunications, namely, Mr. M. E. Bai-grie. It was explained to me by Bell Canada that although the operators involved in this incident are employees of Bell Canada, they are entirely subject to taking orders and instructions from the Government of Canada.
This brings me, Mr. Speaker, directly to my point of privilege, and that is that we have a case proven beyond a doubt that the Government of Canada, through the Department of Communications, is requiring operators to listen to telephone calls being made by members of this House. It does not seem to me to make any difference how it is explained away, checking for conversation, checking to see if a line is still in use, checking to see if conversation is going on: all of these things boil down to one simple, straightforward fact, and that is that people, under instructions of this government, are listening periodically to private telephone calls of members of parliament.
This I contend, Mr. Speaker, is a breach of the law of this country; it is an affront to parliament; it is directly interfering with the privileges of members of parliament, regardless of political affiliation, when they talk to constituents and other persons over the lines of Bell Canada with complete confidentiality expected.
I realize that generally operators of Bell Canada are honest people who are not concerned with reporting what opposition members of parliament are talking about in regard to government policies or other important matters, but the essential thing is that the very fact this listening is going on does not in any way preclude the obvious possibility that there could be those who would, under direct instruction of the government, make notes and report on calls to those in government to whom such calls might be of interest, and this I think is intolerable and quite beyond the democratic process.
A situation which can even permit an opening for any government to spy on the conversations of members of parliament is not one that should be treated lightly. It may be debatable, Mr. Speaker, if this is a definite case of privilege, but I do not believe it is in any way debatable that if it is a matter that is not strictly a case of privilege, it comes very close to it, and I therefore request the Chair's consideration of this matter.
In conclusion, I would also ask the privilege of reserving the right to move a subsequent motion on this subject should such seem to be advisable, since in a democracy anything that smacks remotely of dictatorial wire-tapping, eavesdropping or spying, or which creates a situation where such things could happen, must be stopped and stopped forthwith.

speakeroldname: Mr. Speaker:
speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-ALLEGED TAPPING OF MEMBERS' TELEPHONES
speechtext:
Order, please. The hon. member, of course, raises a very serious point. There have been allusions by two other hon. members of the House on previous days, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) and the hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo (Mr. Beatty), to difficulties not precisely of the same sort but similar difficulties with the technical equipment. After an assurance to the hon. member for Yukon just before the recess, I had a preliminary technical report-prepared, and I think perhaps the most advisable course might be to
October 14, 1975

Since there is a great variation in the placement of CBC network programming on affiliated independent stations, it would take considerable expenditures in order to determine the exact amount of radio listening to CBC network programming via private stations. An extrapolated guesstimate of the reach of CBC programming on affiliated stations is about 1.8 per cent so that the total listening to CBC programming is 8.9 per cent. The term "listening" in the question is not defined. Very often people use the words "total hours tuned" and "total listening" as equivalent. BBM really measures only whether a radio set is on, not whether the listener is really listening, nor to what degree he is engaged in the message being communicated. Many background music stations have high ratings, but whether anyone is really listening is a different question. The CBC on the other hand sends to present programming which by its very nature demands attention. The statistics for the CBC may therefore be deceiving: they indicate 8.9 per cent of tuning, but the CBC may well account for a much higher percentage of all engaged radio listening. There are no statistical measurements of attentive versus non-attentive listening.

subsubtopic: PAYMENT OF CURRENT TAXES ON PENSION PAYMENTS
speechtext: Will consideration be given to allowing an individual to pay current taxes on payments made to compulsory pension plans, thus making the proceeds of the plan non-taxable to the individual that has pre-selected this procedure?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: PAYMENT OF CURRENT TAXES ON PENSION PAYMENTS
speechtext: This proposal is not under consideration since, for almost every taxpayer, it is more advantageous to obtain a deduction during the course of working life when the individual's marginal tax rate is higher, than to pay tax on income after retirement when the marginal tax rate is lower. This advantage has been considerably enchanced by the passage of $1,000 pension exemption. Under the alternative proposed, a taxpayer who utilized such a scheme would get no deduction when his personal income was higher, and would lose the benefit of the $1,000 pension deduction. He would also have lost the income earned on the deferred taxes. It should be noted that such a plan would be very difficult to administer, not only for Revenue Canada, but also for the employers and trustees of such plans, who would have to keep track of the various options made available to their employees.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):

speechtext:
The Energy Supplies Allocation reports as follows: 1. The draft petroleum products allocation plan has not been specifically approved by the cabinet, nor is there any requirement that it be so approved. However, the plan was discussed with all interested departments and agencies of government and received the approval of their officials.
2.	To determine the wholesale customers belonging to the critical category the following criteria were used: the maintenance of health and basic essentials to life; and the protection of individuals and their property. The following criterion was used to determine those wholesale customers who belong in the essential category: the maintenance of the viability of the Canadian economy. The following criterion was used to determine those wholesale customers belonging to the non-essential category: the maintenance of the standard of living enjoyed in Canada.
3.	With respect to propulsion products, i.e. motor gasoline and diesel fuel, farmers were placed in the critical category. The food processing industry was placed in the critical category with respect to heating oils required to process food. The trucking industry was placed in the essential category with respect to propulsion products. The critical need for propulsion for farmers in sowing and
Order Paper Questions
harvesting crops is obvious. The same can be said for the need for heat for food processing, a need which must be met promptly and continuously if food is to be available to Canada's population. The same cannot be said for the trucking industry as a whole. It is recognized that trucks carry products of a critical nature, but they also carry products considered non-essential, such as toys, furniture, automobile parts, etc.
4.	The government does not intend to upgrade the trucking industry to the critical category. Provisions are made in the program for the petroleum industry to supply additional products to those customers in the essential category on an emergency basis. All such deliveries are subject to post facto audits to determine if the wholesale customer in fact needed the additional product. Obviously trucking firms that deal solely with products of the critical category will be similarly treated in terms of fuel supply but it cannot be assumed that since some products they carry are critical, all truckers should be considered critical.

NATIONAL DEFENCE-AIRCRAFT SUPPORT TO OTHER DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
1.	Is it the policy of the government to require the Department of National Defence to meet the requirements for aircraft support of other departments?
2.	For the fiscal year 1975-76, what departments have requested aircraft support from the Department of National Defence and, in each case (a) how many hours and/or days of actual flying time were requested (b) what type of aircraft was sought (c) for what purpose (d) what has been the approved level of support agreed upon by DND if different from the requested amount?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Richardson (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-AIRCRAFT SUPPORT TO OTHER DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
1. Government policy is to provide Canadian Forces aircraft support to other government departments concerned with Canadian Sovereignty and security as set out in the White Paper, Defence in the 70's. However, such support assistance is contingent on DND being able to fulfill its primary defence roles.
2.	(a), (b), (c), (d). For fiscal year 1975/76 the Department of Environment has requested DND for assistance in support of its surveillance and control operations which includes various forms of environmental services and fisheries and marine services. DND plans to cooperate to the fullest extent on the understanding that many of DOE's requirements may have to be ancillary to DND primary defence roles. A total of 915 flying hours (Tracker and Argus Aircraft) are dedicated to DOE programs. For the remainder of DOE's requests it is planned to make arrangements, if possible, to fulfill the requirements with other DND multi-tasked missions. In addition DND pro-

vides short notice airlift support to all other departments, resources permitting. However, the cost for this support is in the majority of cases recoverable from the departments concerned.

ESCAPE OF PRISONERS FROM WILLIAM HEAD MAXIMUM SECURITY PRISON
speechtext:
1.	Did three prisoners escape from William Head Maximum Security Prison at William Head on Vancouver Island in late April or early May,
1975?
2.	Was a security fence recently installed at a cost of $100,000 which was intended to upgrade the outer perimeter protective features of the prison from medium to maximum security standards and, if so, did two of the prisoners escape by walking around the end of the fence?
3.	Is the Prison exposed on the waterside by some 3 1/2 miles of unfenced and otherwise insecure waterfront?
4.	Is any thought being given to relocating the Institution instead of spending some $5,000,000 to "upgrade" the site to afford the law abiding public of the use of some of the finest parkland in the area?

speakeroldname: Hon. Warren Allmand (Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ESCAPE OF PRISONERS FROM WILLIAM HEAD MAXIMUM SECURITY PRISON
speechtext:
It should be noted that William Head Institution is not a maximum security institution; it was upgraded from minimum security to medium security on September 1, 1974. 1. Three inmates walked away, during the month of March 1975, from William Head Institution.
2.	A security fence was installed as one item of various works planned to change the institutional operations from minimum security (unrestricted movement) to medium security with some restriction of movement. In all cases the admimistrative inquiries were unable to ascertain the exact escape route taken by these inmates.
3.	The waterfront of the peninsula on which this institution is located is not fenced. The rough exposed shoreline and the elaborate internal patrol road system are considered an effective deterrent to escape for the inmate transferred to that institution. However, the Canadian Penitentiary Service is planning to form guard-dog foot patrol teams within the perimeter to reinforce the institutional preventive security controls.
4.	There are no plans to relocate the institution as to do so would be much more costly. Upgrading consists of replacing existing buildings and bringing services such as
October 14, 1975

water and sewage treatment up to a standard required by environmental authorities.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PERCENTAGE OF FINANCIAL ASSETS OF INDIVIDUALS HELD IN RESERVES
speechtext: It is not understood what the term "reserves" refers to in the context of this question. The most recent data on financial assets holdings by individuals is contained in the Statistics Canada publication entitled "Incomes, Assets and Indebtedness of Families in Canada", catalogue No. 13-547. This information was compiled from a survey conducted in the spring of 1970. It is not possible to determine the precise shift in the composition of holdings of financial assets of individuals over the past ten years due to the infrequency of the Statistics Canada surveys. The survey preceding the 1970 survey which can be referred to for comparison purposes is entitled "Incomes, Assets and Indebtedness of Non-Farm Families in Canada." The catalogue number for this survey, which was conducted in 1964, is 13-525.

speechtext:

speakerposition: subtopic
Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
1.	Has an investigation been carried out on the incident at the Civic Hospital in Ottawa in March of this year when a person broke into the hospital's storage place for radioactive materials and is reported to have caused damage by spilling radioactive materials?
2.	What was the result of such investigation?
3.	What precautions have been recommended to the Civic Hospital to make sure this does not happen again?
4.	What precautions, if any, are other hospitals in Canada taking to prevent a similar incident?
5.	Was anyone injured or contaminated by radioactive materials as a result of the incident and, if so, what are the details?
6.	How was the area of the Civic Hospital made safe again from radioactive contamination?
Order Paper Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: 1. Yes.
2.	The investigation showed that the lock on the radioisotope laboratory door was defective, that the contamination was isolated to one area of one wing of the hospital, that all radioactive material removed from the laboratory was accounted for, and that nobody was exposed to any significant hazard as a result of the incident.
3.	Recommendations were made to the Civic Hospital concerning improvement of the physical security of the radioisotope laboratory.
4.	As a condition of their licences, hospitals are required to keep radioisotope laboratories locked at all times when not being used. However, as a result of the Civic Hospital incident, the Atomic Energy Control Board is currently reviewing its guidelines on physical security which will be communicated to hospitals and other institutions using radioactive material.
5.	The only person contaminated by radioactive material as a result of the incident was the person who removed the material from the laboratory. He apparently became contaminated when he broke open one of the glass vials which he had removed. He was thoroughly showered and washed within hours with the consequent removal of the contamination. No injuries resulted.
6.	The affected area of the Civic Hospital was thoroughly washed to remove the radioactive contamination. A few items, which were difficult to wash such as a chair and a telephone, were stored until the radioactivity decayed to acceptable levels.

speakerposition: subtopic
Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: With respect to the answer to Question No. 1,720 which stated that "radioactive wastes which are permitted to be poured down the sinks of hospitals generally have short radioactive half-lives", and that "they rapidly decay before they can accumulate to detectable levels in the water supply and the life cycle of humans" (a) what are such wastes that are disposed of in this way (b) what are the half-lives of such wastes (c) what, if any, are the substances disposed of in this way that are not "general" (d) what are the "detectable levels" referred to by the Atomic Energy Control Board (e) how are these levels monitored near hospitals to make sure that they are below "detectable levels" (f) how are these levels monitored to make sure that they do not get into the life cycle of human beings?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: (a) Examples of the wastes referred to in this question are solutions of iodine, technetium or gold, (b) Iodine 131 has a half-life of eight days; technetium 99m has a half-life of 6 hours; and gold 198 has a half-life of 65 hours, (c) Some materials are used less frequently than the above isotopes because of recent changes in clinical needs. speakerposition: subtopic
Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
1.	How do scientists at the University of British Columbia dispose of radioactive (a) liquids (b) solids (c) gases (d) biological wastes?
2.	How are such radioactive wastes (a) moved (b) stored?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: 1. (a) Liquid radioactive wastes at the University of British Columbia are disposed of by dilution and discharge to the sewage system, (b) Solid radioactive wastes at the University of British Columbia are disposed of by being shipped to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, Chalk River, Ontario. Low level wastes containing only trace quantities of radioactive material are incinerated on campus, depending on the type of waste, (c) Gaseous radioactive wastes at the University of British Columbia are discharged to the atomosphere (in such a manner that permissible concentrations in air breathed by personnel are not exceeded), (d) Biological radioactive wastes at the University of British Columbia are incinerated.
2.	(a) Wastes are transported on campus in a University of British Columbia truck used specifically for the carriage of "dangerous" materials. All such wastes are double bagged in polyethylene, checked for contamination and radiation levels, and suitably labelled, (b) Solid wastes are stored, pending shipment to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, in a special concrete central waste storage facility.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):

speechtext: Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: Nuclear power plants are designed to withstand any credible earthquake or explosion that could occur at the site. speakerposition: subtopic
Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: Do some radioactive wastes from CANDU reactors have a half-life of up to 25,000 years and do the currently designed storage vessels have an estimated life of 100 years and, if so, does the government feel confident that a longer term storage system will soon be devised for these dangerous wastes?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: Some of the radioactive materials contained in the spent fuel discharged from CANDU reactors are very long-lived. For example, plutonium-239 requires about 250,000 years (i.e. ten half-lives) to decay to a negligible level. At present, the spent fuel is stored retrievably in interim surface storage facilities pending decisions on re-use and ultimate storage or disposal. Several possibilities for ultimate storage or disposal of radioactive wastes are currently under investigation in Canada, including burial in geologic formations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: NUCLEAR REACTORS AND HEAVY WATER PLANTS
speechtext:
1.	How many nuclear reactors and heavy water plants are projected for Canada up to the year 2000 and (a) where will each be located (b) what is the estimated amount of radioactive wastes that will have accumulated by that time?
2.	What training programmes are being devised to acquire personnel to staff such operations?
3.	(a) Are trained personnel available locally to the plants (b) will talent have to be imported and, if so, from where?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: NUCLEAR REACTORS AND HEAVY WATER PLANTS
speechtext:
1.	Atomic Energy of Canada Limited estimates that about 115 nuclear reactors will be located in Canada up to the year 2000. Because the vast majority of these will be owned and operated by provincial utilities, the actual number will be determined more by the provincial governments than by the federal government. AECL estimates that eight to 12 heavy water plants, each capable of producing about 800 tons of heavy water annually, will be required in Canada by the year 2000. The actual number installed will be determined partly by experience gained through operation

of current plants and partly by the rate of installation of nuclear reactors, (a) The location of each of these nuclear reactors and heavy water plants will be determined by the utility or private company that owns the plant, subject to the approval of appropriate federal or provincial boards or departments, (b) It is estimated that about 125,000 megagrams of radioactive waste in the form of spent fuel will have been accumulated by the year 2000.
2.	To date, personnel to staff such operations have been trained either in facilities owned and operated by the plant owners or in the facilities of other utilities such as Ontario Hydro or Hydro Quebec.
3.	(a) Experience to date indicates that personnel capable of being trained to operate such plants can be found within the province in which the plant is located, (b) The possibility of having to import talent into Canada to operate such plants seems very remote.

speechtext:

2.	Has an analysis been made to determine the costs involved in re-using plutonium as reactor fuel in Canada?
3.	Are the environmental public health and safety risks greater when plutonium is re-used as a fuel in a reactor?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:

Atomic Energy of Canada Limited has just begun a long-term development program to determine answers to the many technological, economic and social questions that might arise should a future shortage or uranium indicate the desirability of installing reactors that use plutonium in the fuel cycle.
2.	An analysis of the costs involved in reusing plutonium as reactor fuel is one of the objectives of the development program.
3.	The environmental, public health and safety risks associated with the reuse of plutonium as fuel in a reactor are among the major questions to be answered by the development program.

speechtext: Atomic Energy of Canada Limited reports as follows: (a) Those parts which must be replaced prior to decommissioning of the entire reactor and are not radioactive are disposed of in the normal industrial manner. speakerposition: subtopic
Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: What are the guarantees that CANDU nuclear generating systems will not be subject to human error?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: The safety philosophy for CANDU nuclear power plants is based on "defence-in-depth"; that is, the public would be protected even if several human errors and/or equipment failures were to occur. Just as important, however, is the fact that CANDU nuclear power plants are designed and constructed to high standards and the operators are trained to high standards to minimize the probability of serious human errors and equipment failures.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):

speechtext:
Atomic Energy of Canada Limited reports as follows: 1. Over the past two years an extensive and detailed survey has been done to determine the potential value of thorium in CANDU reactors. 2.	Yes, thorium could be used in a standard CANDU reactor with fairly minor modifications that could be retrofitted to the reactor. speechtext:

2.	What has been the cost to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
1.	Atomic Energy of Canada Limited has co-operated fully with Ontario Hydro in solving the pressure tube leak

problem at Pickering. This co-operation has taken two forms: (i) AECL has provided design services and equipment development services for locating the leaking pressure tubes, for removing these from the reactor and for replacing them with new pressure tubes. Most of this work was done at AECL's Power Projects site in Toronto; (ii) AECL has undertaken to discover the reasons why the leaks developed in the pressure tube and to determine how to avoid the problem on future reactions. Most of this work is being done at AECL's research centres at Chalk River and Whiteshell.

The cost of this latter work is taken from AECL's annual operating budget.

speechtext: With reference to the answer to Question No. 1,724, which stated the Department of Energy Mines and Resources has "no definite knowledge" of a statement widely reported in the media that an official of Ontario Hydro said in a press conference about the Pickering radioactive leaks that many worse things have happened, does the government or any agency of the government have any knowledge of any incident involving nuclear technology in Canada that was worse than the Pickering leaks?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: We cannot speculate as to what the unnamed Ontario Hydro official meant by "worse things have happened". The Douglas Point Generating Station was the first commercial scale CANDU nuclear-electric station and is considered a prototype. Some difficulties were expected even though great effort was made to avoid them. The success of the Pickering Generating Station is largely due to the lessons learned at the Douglas Point Generating Station and the earlier, small scale, Nuclear Power Demonstration Generating Station.

speakerposition: subtopic
Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
1.	What studies have been done on the Ottawa River to investigate levels of radioactivity from the Chalk River waste disposal unit?
2.	What were the results of such studies and are they a matter of public record?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
1.	There is continuous surveillance of the Ottawa River by the Department of National Health & Welfare in collaboration with the Ontario Department of Health and the Ontario Ministry of the Environment. Atomic Energy of Canada Limited also carries out its own environmental monitoring program on the river. The Department of National Health & Welfare program analyses drinking water at five locations along the river, both upstream and down-
Order Paper Questions
stream from the Chalk River Nuclear Laboratories. In addition, fish are collected both upstream and downstream and analysed. Wildlife samples are also taken periodically. The AECL program monitors soil, water, air and vegetation in the vicinity of the waste management areas and all effluents. In addition, it operates a completely independent drinking water monitoring program at Rolphton, Deep River and Pembroke. Other special studies are carried out from time to time on bottom sediments, fish and aquatic plants (water weeds).
2.	Generally speaking, results of studies show that the Chalk River Laboratories contribute minor amounts of radionuclides to the Ottawa River relative to the natural and bomb fallout radionuclides already present. Levels of radioactivity in the drinking water at Pembroke are indistinguishable from background levels. AECL results show that the average concentration of radioactivity in any of the effluents from the laboratory-before reaching the river-is less than 1 per cent of the occupational limit for drinking water. The data are published quarterly in detail in the open scientific literature.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: LEAKAGE OF RADIOACTIVE WASTE NEAR COLUMBIA RIVER IN USA

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: LEAKAGE OF RADIOACTIVE WASTE NEAR COLUMBIA RIVER IN USA
speechtext: To the knowledge of the government, have over 400,000 gallons of radioactive waste been leaked from storage tanks in the State of Washington in the United States near the Columbia River since 1958 and, if so (a) has the government undertaken any studies to see if any of this material was flowing north into British Columbia (b) what was the result of such studies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LEAKAGE OF RADIOACTIVE WASTE NEAR COLUMBIA RIVER IN USA
speechtext:
Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: (a) Large quantities of radioactive liquid wastes have, on occasion, leaked from storage tanks at the Hanford site. These incidents have been reported in the press and in technical publications, (b) The Hanford site is in an arid, desert-like area of Washington State. We understand from the literature that all of the radioactivity has been trapped in the soil adjacent to the storage tanks and none of the radioactivity has penetrated down to the water table which, at Hanford, is over a hundred feet below the maximum depth of penetration of the radioactive materials. The nearest significant body of water is the Columbia River which is 8 miles away from the tanks. The Columbia River does not flow back into Canada but flows to the Pacific Ocean at a point over one hundred miles from the Canadian border (measured along the shoreline to the Strait of Juan de Fuca). The ocean currents in the area flow from north to south. A number of communities including Portland, Oregon, are located on the Columbia River downstream of the Hanford site. To the best of our knowledge, U.S. officials have no fear that the leaks at Hanford represent any threat to those communities because none of the radioactive materials have reached the river and none are likely to reach it in the future. Based on all the above factors, it is evident that no useful purpose would be served by any studies to see if any of the radioactive material is flowing north into British Columbia.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board

1.	With reference to the answer to Question No. 1,713 (a) how much plutonium has Canada sold to France (b) on what dates?
2.	How was the plutonium transported (a) across Canada and (b) to France and, what safeguards, if any, were taken to make sure the shipments were not vandalized, sabotaged or stolen?
3.	What safeguards are taken to protect public health and safety from any and all mishaps while plutonium is in transit?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LEAKAGE OF RADIOACTIVE WASTE NEAR COLUMBIA RIVER IN USA
speechtext:
Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: 1. Irradiated fuel bundles from the Nuclear Power Demonstration and Douglas Point Generating Stations have been sold to France. These fuel bundles which contained approximately 120 kilograms of plutonium were shipped from Canada between August 1969 and May 1972.
2.	The irradiated fuel bundles were removed from the storage ponds at the Chalk River Nuclear Laboratories and Douglas Point and loaded into approved shipping containers. These containers travelled by specially arranged and approved road transport to Toronto and Montreal where they were loaded aboard a ship and transported to Belgium where the reprocessing plant chosen by the French Government is located.
3.	All shipments of irradiated fuel are made under regulations issued by the Atomic Energy Control Board. In the case of this shipment, the details of the proposed shipping arrangements including design and construction of the flask, proposed routing, loading, cleaning and monitoring procedures, were all submitted to the Atomic Energy Control Board for approval. Permission for the transfer was only issued after a thorough review indicated that the risk to public health and safety was acceptable in conformance with prevailing international standards.

speechtext: Has any uranium or plutonium been missing or unaccounted for (a) in transit from Canada (b) produced by Canadian-built reactors in other countries?

speechtext: (a) The Atomic Energy Control Board is aware of no incident where uranium or plutonium has been missing or unaccounted for in transit from Canada, (b) The Atomic Energy Control Board is aware of no situation where uranium or plutonium used or produced in Canadian-built reactors which are under bilateral or international safeguards in other countries has been missing or unaccounted for.

speechtext: What safeguards does the government provide to ensure that radioactive materials in transit will not be hijacked (a) within Canada (b) during export from Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SAFEGUARDS FOR NUCLEAR MATERIALS IN TRANSIT
speechtext:
Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: The security arrangements provided by the federal government to ensure that radioactive materials in transit will not be

hijacked within Canada or during export from Canada are specially arranged for each shipment and tailored to reflect the quantity and form of the material being shipped. speakerposition: subtopic
Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: With reference to the answer to Question No. 1,731 which stated that 2,204.6 pounds of plutonium are produced each year at the Pickering CANDU reactor, what assurances can the government provide that this material will not be stolen and used for criminal activities in (a) Canada (b) countries that are purchasing CANDU reactors?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: (a) The plutonium produced in the Pickering reactors is at present contained in irradiated fuel bundles stored in the spent fuel storage pond at the Pickering Reactor Generating Station. These bundles, which are highly radioactive, are stored under approximately 20 feet of water and cannot be removed from this storage pond without a skilled team of technicians and operators and specially built equipment including special transportation containers which weigh from 25 to 50 tons. The physical characteristics of the fuel bundles and existing security precautions are deemed to provide adequate protection, (b) The precise physical security precautions applied to CANDU reactors abroad by foreign nations are chosen by the nation in question. Canada has assisted the International Atomic Energy Agency in the preparation of international guides to physical security standards as part of its general effort to ensure that adequate physical protection measures are in place in all nuclear facilities around the world not only in CANDU reactors.

speakerposition: subtopic
Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: Are twenty-two pounds of plutonium enough to produce an atomic bomb and, if not, how many pounds are required?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: The exact quantity of plutonium required to produce a nuclear bomb or explosive is dependent on the isotopic content, the purity, density and other physical characteristics of the plutonium but most important on the design and fabrication of the nuclear weapon concerned. The effect of each of the potential variables and the minimum quantity required to produce a nuclear bomb are carefully guarded military secrets which are not known in Canada. In order to establish levels of security precautions, the Atomic Energy Control Board has assumed that a nuclear explosive device could be assembled from 15 pounds of plutonium.

speakerposition: subtopic
Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Are high doses of radioactive exposure known to cause death or cancer and, if so, is there any information on the long-term effects of low-level radioactive exposure?
October 14, 1975

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. High doses of radiation can cause cancer and they can cause death as well. Cancers have been observed following doses in the order of 100 rems or more received either in a short period or spread over a long period. The cancer does not appear immediately but after a latent period of several months to many years after the exposure. Deaths due to non-cancerous injuries may result from doses of 200 to 700 rems received in a short period. Exposures of such magnitude may result in death within a few weeks of the exposure, whereas more rapid deaths (within hours) require thousands of rems received in a short period. Taking "low level exposure" to means exposures received within the legal dose limits (5 rems per year to the whole body, for example), there have been no observable effects. It is assumed, for regulatory purposes, that effects are proportional to dose (even at low doses and low doe rates) but this remains an assumption, for no effects have been observed.

speakerposition: subtopic
Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: What is the acceptable level of radioactive exposure (a) for a person's lifetime (b) for a year (c) in one exposure?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: (a)-(c) The levels of radiation exposure to the whole body permitted by the Atomic Energy Control Regulations are (in addition to natural background radiation and radiation from medical exposures): for atomic'radiation workers-up to 3 rems in a single exposure but no more than 3 rems per quarter of a year and no more than 5 rems for a year; in a working lifetime, say 50 years, the accumulated dose could be 250 rems. For members of the public-the level permitted by the Atomic Energy Control Regulations is no more than .05 rem/year to the whole body. In principle, this could be received in a single exposure, but in practice, any dose received by members of the public is likely to be spread out more or less uniformally during th year. In a lifetime (say 70 years), the accumulated dose could be as high as 35 rems. In practice, it is assured, through the licencing actions of the Atomic Energy Control Board, that the highest exposed members of the public generally receive no more than about 1 per cent of the doses permitted by the Atomic Energy Control Regulations.

subtopic: PROTECTION OF WORKERS AT NUCLEAR FACILITIES

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: PROTECTION OF WORKERS AT NUCLEAR FACILITIES
speechtext:
1.	(a) How many workers at nuclear facilities in Canada are exposed to radioactive materials (b) what is the extent of their exposure?
2.	What safeguards exist to protect the health of workers?
3.	Are workers in nuclear facilities given regular medical check-ups or other tests to ascertain the degree of their exposure?
4.	Are workers protected under an insurance plan against exposure to radioactive materials?
5.	Can a worker in a nuclear facility who is contaminated by radioactive wastes seek damages from his employer?
6.	Has any member of a family of a worker at a nuclear facility in Canada become contaminated with radioactive material as a result of the worker becoming contaminated?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROTECTION OF WORKERS AT NUCLEAR FACILITIES
speechtext:
Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: 1. Approximately 2,500 workers may be regularly exposed to ionizing radiation at nuclear facilities in Canada. Most of these workers receive a radiation dose of less than half the statutory limits.
2.	Measures to protect the radiological health of atomic radiation workers are stipulated in the Atomic Energy Control Regulations. Where necessary, these measures are further specified in the licences issued by the Atomic Energy Control Board. These measures include requirements for minimizing, measuring and recording the exposure of such workers to ionizing radiation.
3.	Yes. Atomic radiation workers are given medical tests of a type and frequency prescribed by medical advisers to the Atomic Energy Control Board. The degree of their radiation exposure, that is, radiation dose, is measured primarily by personal radiation dosimeters and by analysis of urine samples. The amount of radiation dose permitted at nuclear facilities is so low that medical effects are not a useful guide to radiation dose. Indeed, the regulatory limits have been chosen so as to prevent medical effects from occurring.
4.	Yes. Workers are covered by Workmens' Compensation.
5.	Traditionally, workers who are convered by Workmens' Compensation cannot sue their employer; however, when the Nuclear Liability Act is proclaimed, workers who suffer personal injury as a result of radiation exposure can sue the operator (as defined by the act) for damages; and the operator is absolutely liable for any breach of his duty under the act.
6.	There have been cases in the past of workers at nuclear facilities in Canada who have worn contaminated clothing to their home. In such cases, there were no detectable medical consequences to the worker or to members of his family.

speakerposition: subtopic
Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: To the knowledge of the government, has the United States approved guidelines that will expose the public in that country to 100 times less radiation than is the acceptable limit from reactors in Canada and, if so, is Canada considering similar measures?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: Both the

October 14, 1975
Order Paper Questions
United States and the Canadian regulations defining permissible limits of radiation exposure to occupationally-exposed workers and to members of the general public are based on the recommendations of the International Commission on Radiological Protection. The statutory limits in Canada and the U.S.A. are the same. In addition to recommending numerical limits, the International Commission on Radiological Protection cautions that exposures should be kept "as low as is readily achievable, economic and social considerations being taken into account". The United States Nuclear Regulatory Commission has issued guidelines governing the release of radioactive effluents from light-water-cooled nuclear power reactors. The effect of these guidelines is that the resultant radiation dose to members of the public should not exceed about 1% of the statutory dose limits. In advance of the United States action, the Canadian regulatory agency, the Atomic Energy Control Board, established design and operating targets such that the radiation dose to members of the public resulting from radioactive effluents from nuclear power stations and other nuclear facilities and devices should not exceed 1% of the statutory dose limits specified in the Atomic Energy Control Regulations. The operating experience at the Pickering Generating Station indicates that these targets are being achieved.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Did employees at the Pickering nuclear facility receive radioactive exposure in excess of 5 Rems and, if so, how many were involved?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: Very few people, perhaps three or four per year, receive more than 5 rem/year and the doses received by these people have been all less than 10 rem/year. It should be noted that up to 10 rems per year can be permitted by the Atomic Energy Control Board under the Atomic Energy Control Regulations since a dose of 10 rems is not considered to be excessive as long as the dose averaged from age 18 up to the current exposure period does not exceed 5 rems per year.

speakerposition: subtopic
Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: Has the International Commission on Radiological Protection set an arbitrary figure of about 5 Rems as the maximum acceptable radioactive exposure to a human being over 30 years, and has the United States recently reduced this acceptability figure by a factor of 100 per cent and, if so, is the government reviewing the acceptable radiation exposure figure in Canada to come into line with the United States figure?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: The International Commission on Radiological Protection has set a tentative limit of 5 rems per generation on the genetically significant dose to a population, assuming that a generation is of 30 years duration. This limit is included in the Canadian Atomic Energy Control Regulations. Neither has the U.S. established a limit based on genetically significant dose; however, the U.S has used a number

which is numerically equivalent to 5 rems per 30 years, but this numer (0.17 rem/year) is based on somatic rather than genetic effects. As stated in the answer to question No.
2.749,	the United States Nuclear Regulatory Commission recently established numerical guidelines for design objectives governing the release of radioactive effluents from light-water-cooled nuclear reactors. These guidelines are quite separate and distinct from the 5 rem per generation figure referred to above and apply to the statutory dose limits specified by the United States Nuclear Regulatory Commission. As also stated in the answer to question No.
2.749,	the action taken by the United States is essentially the same as that taken by the Atomic Energy Control Board of Canada in 1974. Accordingly, it is incorrect to suggest that the acceptable dose limits in the U.S. are lower by a factor of 100 than the applicable Canadian limits.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

The most recent Atomic Energy of Canada Limited studies concerning the relationship between genetic risks and exposure to ionizing radiation suggest that less of the genetic disease in human populations is of a kind that increases with radiation than was formerly believed to be the case. speechtext: With reference to the annual report of the AECL which states "waste management is an important part of the nuclear program" and a "significant effort" will be made to make sure that "ultimate solutions are optimum in terms of public acceptance", will the government be starting a programme of public information to set before the people the alternatives so that public acceptance will reflect informed public opinion?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows; The development of a radioactive waste management program is more than a technical matter. The management process includes matters of regulatory policy and responsibility at various levels of government and also the broader consideration of the responsibilities which present generations can be allowed to bequeath to future generations.
