speechtext: With reference to the answer to Question No. 1,715 stating that the government is committed to the development of nuclear energy in Canada (a) what discussions, if any, did the government undertake with environmentalist or other groups before taking such decision (b) were the people of Canada, in the opinion of the government fully informed of the risks involved in the development of nuclear energy and of the alternative future sources of energy before the decision was taken?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The Department of Energy, Mines and Resources reports as follows: (a) The Canadian government's support for the development of nuclear energy in Canada extends back in time for three decades. As early as 1945 commitments were made to convert the war-time legacy of nuclear energy to peaceful purposes. The major reasons were to provide access to the enormous store of energy in Canadian uranium and to enable Canada to compete in an increasingly technological world. In 1946, the government of the day, aware of the possible risks inherent in nuclear technology, promulgated the Atomic Energy Control Act and formed
October 14, 1975

the Atomic Energy Control Board to regulate the industry in terms of public health and reactor safety. At that time no environmental protection organizations were taking any interest in this area. Nonetheless, government and industry were making every effort to carefully protect the environment and to keep the public fully informed. Continuous programs of public education on nuclear power have been carried out, for example, by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Ontario Hydro since the start-up of the Nuclear Power Demonstration reactor at Rolphton in 1962. Since the recent development of organized public interest in this field and the formation of new groups, however, many discussions both public and private have taken place, and many questions asked by such groups have been answered to their apparent satisfaction by the Atomic Energy Control Board, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick electric utilities, (b) In view of the foregoing, it is clear that consultation with the people of Canada has been taking place on a continuous basis since the start of this development. Recently, for example, an environmental assessment was completed of the proposed New Brunswick Point Lepreau Nuclear Station by a panel of experts led by the Department of the Environment. A public meeting was held to review the report and many public briefs were presented. Conditional environmental approval for the reactor was given by the Department of the Environment on the basis of all this information. Had Canada not gone ahead as she did, U.S. light water reactors would now be the major alternative source of energy. An industry employing tens of thousands would not exist, Canada would not have the very successful Pickering Generating Station and would not be in the forefront of technological development in this field.

subtopic: ACQUISITION OF LANDS FOR NATIONAL WILDLIFE AREAS
speechtext: In regard to the current controversy surrounding the potentially dangerous effect of fluorocarbons on the earth's ozone layer, is the Minister considering banning the use of aerosol cans?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ACQUISITION OF LANDS FOR NATIONAL WILDLIFE AREAS
speechtext: Aerosol cans as well as other uses of fluorocarbons have been under review for some time. The assessment of Canadian scientists, based on a theoretical model, is that the fluorocarbons may pose a threat to the ozone layer. However, precise measurements of key chemical constituents in the stratosphere and other research are required in order to draw firm conclusions regarding the nature and seriousness of the threat. A decision on whether to restrict use of fluorocarbons in aerosol cans should be possible in one to two years depending on progress in making the necessary scientific measurements.

CRITERIA USED TO DETERMINE BUILDING OF FEDERAL BUILDINGS
speechtext:
1.	What criteria are used to determine whether a federal building will be constructed in a town or city?
2.	Has consideration been given to the construction of a federal building in Spruce Grove or Leduc, Alberta?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: CRITERIA USED TO DETERMINE BUILDING OF FEDERAL BUILDINGS
speechtext:
1. In
general, the following criteria are used to determine whether a government of Canada building will be constructed in a town or city; (i) There must be a specific request by one or more federal departments or agencies for space in a particular locality or an economic advantage may have been identified in the regrouping of federal departments and agencies from existing accommodation, either Crown-owned or leased. Given a long-term growth projection for a community the eventual construction of Crown-owned facilities would generally be the optimum solution, although rented accommodation is often used in response to requirements for immediate additional accommodation. (ii) Within the context of economic viability a choice is made among various alternative solutions not restricted soley to Crown construction such as leasing, lease-purchase and build-to-lease. However, the economic factor is not necessarily the ultimate criteria as consideration must also be given to other objectives within the context of broader social, environmental, and other considerations.
2. The Department of Public Works has entered into a five-year lease, commencing November 1, 1974, for approximately 4,472 square feet of post office accommodation in Spruce Grove, Alberta. The department recognizes the rapid population growth in the area and a decision will be made well before 1979 on the alternative solutions available to satisfy the requirements of various federal government departments and agencies in Spruce Grove. A government of Canada building already exists in Leduc, Alberta, which is adequate in so far as current and projected federal accommodation requirements are concerned. At the present time the Department of Public Works is renovating the ground floor to meet post office requirements.

Emergency plans were prepared in all these institutions in conjunction with the Department of National Defence and the police forces, and dynamic security training programs were initiated. speechtext: Did the government conduct or finance any studies on the subject of subliminal advertising in either the electronic or print media and, if so (a) by whom were they conducted (b) what were their conclusions (c) what was the nature of the work done (d) on what date were they completed (e) what was their cost (f) what action has resulted from their recommendations (g) from whom can copies be obtained?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: STUDIES ON SUBJECT OF SUBLIMINAL ADVERTISING
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of Communications is concerned: no. In so far as the Canadian Radio-Television Commission is concerned: The Canadian Radio-Television Commission did not commission studies on subliminal advertising. However, in preparation for a public hearing on the subject, held on March 11th, 1975, an independent legal opinion and study of the status of subliminal advertising in other countries was obtained. The Research Branch of the Commission conducted a review of all existing studies on subliminal advertising. Both these documents were considered, in addition to the briefs submitted prior to the public hearing. These latter public representations are available from the Public Hearing Section of the CRTC Licensing Branch. As a result of the public hearing, the commission announced the following amendments to the Television Broadcasting Regulations on June 27, 1975: 1. The Television Broadcasting Regulations are amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 9 thereof, the following section: "9.1 (1) No station or network operator shall knowingly broadcast any advertising material that makes use of any subliminal device. (2) In subsection (1), "subliminal device" means a technical device that is used to convey or attempt to convey a message to a person by means of images or sounds of very brief duration or by any other means without that person being aware that such a device is being used or being aware of the substance of the message being conveyed or attempted to be conveyed."

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT "AN INTERIM REPORT ON FREIGHT TRANSPORTATION IN CANADA"
speechtext:
(a) The specific select commodity groups included were iron ore, coal, grain, general cargo (including containers) and forest products, (b) The first column of Exhibit 24 would more properly be headed "Estimated Volume

October 14, 1975

Loaded 1971". The sources for the grain, iron ore, coal, forest products and general cargo commodity groups were Appendices B-l, B-2, B-3, B-5 and B-9 respectively of the January 22nd, 1975 draft Forecast Transportation Flows and Capacity Requirements 1990 prepared by the Transportation Development Agency. The original sources for the commodity data are the Shipping Report Part IV, 1971, Statistics Canada Catalogue No. 54-206 and the Shipping Report Part V, 1971, Statistics Canada Catalogue No. 54-207. However, a number of aggregations and estimates were made using these figures. These qualifications are listed on the following page: Appendix B-l-All Grains: All data are from Statistics Canada 54-207 but flows to Canadian ports are aggregated with the nearest large port so that, for example, Thunder Bay-Toronto flows include flows to Kingston, Collingwood, etc. Appendix B-2-Iron Ore: Vancouver and certain Sept lies iron ore data were provided by the Canadian Transport Commission Systems Analysis branch. Vancouver includes Tasu (British Columbia) etc. Toronto designates the port of Picton and Sudbury designates Depot Harbour and Little Current. All data except Vancouver and Sept lies originate from Statistics Canada 54-207. Appendix B-3-Coal: All data are from SC 54-207. Aggregation again is used with, for example, Toronto being used as a designation for the Southeastern Ontario ports, including most importantly Port Credit. Appendix B-5-Forest Products: Cargo loaded figures were estimated by adding the newsprint and pulpwood figures given in Statistics Canada 54-207 and multiplying by 10/7. Cargo imported figures came from direct aggregation of forest products in Statistics Canada 54-206. Appendix B-9-All Other Commodities: Data are obtained by subtracting figures in B-l through B-8 from Statistics Canada 54-206 numbers for the major ports. Clearly this is a rough estimate since the tables B-l to B-8 have ports representing large areas, but 54-206 does not. In compiling the first column of Exhibit 24 the figures in table B-9, All Other Commodities, were used as a proxy for general cargo. In fact, the general cargo figures that were included, by mistake inconsistently included cargo loaded, and cargo unloaded from certain origins. In addition, Exhibit 24 does not include revisions and corrections made in the final version of the TDA report, Forecast Freight Transportation Flows and Capacity Deficiencies 1990, dated April 1975. Finally, some small differences remain between the TDA Appendix B and the Shipping Report which are a result of approximations or minor inaccuracies.

3.	Basic information on washroom use is needed to develop satisfactory building standards. Local standards differ in their requirements by factors up to 22, i.e. one authority requires 1 fixture, where another authority requires 22. It is estimated that more than $1 million a year could be saved in plazas alone by improving building standards.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REGULATIONS RESPECTING PSYCHOLOGICAL TESTING OF GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES AND POTENTIAL EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
am informed by the Department of National Health and Welfare and Treasury Board Secretariat as follows: 1. Psychological testing is a part of the Public Service Health program that is available to all departments and agencies that fall under the Financial Administration Act. It is also available to Crown corporations who request services from National Health and Welfare.
2.	(a) The purpose of testing is to aid in establishing a health profile or diagnosis in the assessment of an employee's health status as it relates to the safe, healthy, and effective performance of his duties. (It is important to emphasize the difference between psychological testing, and psychological assessment. Psychological testing is done by utilizing a whole battery of tests and aims at something in particular, such as behaviorial pattern. Psychological assessment may be a part of any comprehensive medical examination), (b) There is no routine psychological testing done on categories of employees. In any assessment of the health of some groups of employees, however, particular attention is directed to a psychological assessment because of the nature of the work. These groups are: 1. Personnel posted to isolated posts. 2. Lightkeepers, including dependents resident at remote locations. 3. Personnel serving abroad (including dependents), (c) Tests are administered by a psychiatrist or psychologist, (d) Interpretation is by the health professional who administers the tests, (e) Specialty qualifications as established by the governing body of the profession.
3.	(a) Refusal would result in the Department of National Health and Welfare reporting to a department that an accurate or complete assessment of the employee's health status is impossible to make due to incomplete data. The effect of incomplete health profiles on the employability of an individual is impossible to assess since National Health and Welfare exercises no control over staffing authorities in the manner of employment or promotions, (b) The individual has a right to know the results of any examination by the Department of National Health and Welfare either through direct discussion with the Health and Welfare professional, or where it is deemed in his best interest, through a full disclosure to a physician of the employee's choice, (c) No separate psychological test files are maintained on individuals. However, the results of an individual's psychological test are maintained as part of his/her medical files. Medical files are kept in strict confidentiality by the Medical Services Branch. They are kept active for two years, then dormant for three. After this five year period, they are destroyed, (d) In Medical Services, nine regions are in possession of files of this nature and the number can reach in the tens of thousands; to give an accurate figure would require intensive time and manpower and would be a serious cost to this branch.
4.	Question No. 2,402 part 2(c) was not replied to by the Department of National Health and Welfare since the
[Mr. Beatty.)
question was interpreted as applying to the Department itself and to no other area of the government.
5.	Treasury Board regulations and requirements respecting health evaluations, including psychological assessments where applicable, of employees of departments or other portions of the Public Service of Canada listed in Part 1 of Schedule A to the Public Service Staff Regulations Act, are provided for in the Foreign Service Directives, the Isolated Posts Regulations and in the Public Service Periodic Health Evaluation Standard.

speechtext:
1.	Does the government collect information on emigration from Canada?
2.	What factors (age, sex, nationality, occupation, etc.) are collected in emigration statistics?
3.	Are such data collected by cooperation with the countries of destination and, if not, how are they collected?
4.	Where are these emigration statistics published?
5.	Does the government intend to increase the collection of emigration data and, if so, in what areas?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Statistics Canada reports the following: 1. Like most countries in the world, Canada does not collect data on the number of persons emigrating from the country, because Canadian residents are not compelled to notify provincial or national officials of their departure. However, Statistics Canada produces estimates of the number of persons who emigrate from Canada each year.
2.	The annual estimates of emigration are produced by age group, sex, and province or territory of origin.
3.	The emigration estimates are obtained by adding: (a) actual data from the United States Department of Justice on the number of persons immigrating to the United States whose last country of residence was Canada: (b) actual data from the United Kingdom Office of Population Censuses and Surveys on the number of persons migrating to the United Kingdom wrhose last country of residence was Canada; and (c) an assumed volume of 20,000 persons who are believed to emigrate to all other countries from Canada

each year. The figure 20,000, is based on data in the United Nations Demographic Year Book and differences between the number of post-war immigrants recorded in the 1961 Census and the total post-war immigration figures reported by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
4.	These emigration estimates are compiled for purposes of producing the official post-censal national and provincial population estimates. Although the emigration estimates have not been published, they are made available to individuals who request them.
5.	For the past two years, Canada has been cooperating with the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe in a pilot project the aim of which is to generate current, reliable data on the number of persons migrating between the 32 member countries of the Economic Commission for Europe. Although the results from this pilot project have been encouraging the Economic Commission for Europe is continuing its developmental work on this project before setting up a system for the regular exchange of these data among the member countries. Once this programme becomes fully operational, the data on immigration to these countries from Canada will enable Statistics Canada to generate increasingly accurate and more detailed current emigration estimates.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the answer to starred question No. 2,246 is lengthy, I ask the House to consent to the answer being printed in Hansard as if read.

Agreed.
[Editor's Note: Answer above referred to reads as follows.]
1. The National Harbours Board hat delegated some authority to an Executive Committee of the Montreal Port Authority with respect to the day-to-day operations at the Port of Montreal in the area of personnel, leases, work contracts, service contracts, purchases, rental of equipment, budgets, marketing, public relations, travel and claims.
2.	The Minutes of the National Harbours Board reflect the decisions of the Chairman and Members who are responsible for the administrative management and control of the property under the Board's jurisdiction. The National Harbours Board ports are in competition with other ports both within Canada and in the United States. It is therefore not considered to be in the best interest of either the National Harbours Board or Canada to make such decisions a matter of public information, since many are related to on-going and sometimes confidential business arrangements.
3.	Extracts of Minutes of meetings of the Board are made available to the Courts for such action as the swearing in or dismissal of police constables or for the transfer of property but are not made public by way of any further distribution. All Minutes of the meetings are available to the Minister of Transport when required.
4.	The National Harbours Board is responsible to Parliament through the Minister of Transport. The Board advises the Minister on all policy matters which are felt to be in the public interest in fulfilment of its responsibility to Parliament and the people of Canada, recognizing its role
October 14, 1975

as a Crown Corporation in competition for business with comparable organizations both within and outside Canada. The Minister of Transport determines the extent to which such policy matters should be made public and at what time in their development.
5.	The adoption of a specific policy is not required, since the matters coming to the attention of the Minister of Transport related to disclosure may vary and are subject to the Minister's determination.
8.	Yes.
Insofar as the Ministry of Transport is concerned:
6.	The Minister of Transport, who has responsibility for the National Harbours Board, determines which policy decisions should be made public. He also decides where public participation and feed back will be helpful in policy formulation or changes. Implicit in these decisions is the desire to advance the public image of the Government as well as the Board.
7.	There is no secrecy in the execution of the present port policies or in consideration of a new ports policy, although some matters have to be confidential during developmental stages.

7.	Should U.S. egg prices rise to provide an incentive for increased exports of eggs from Canada to the U.S.A., the Export and Import Permits Act would be used to protect supply and maintain reasonable prices in Canada.

9.	Current egg production is keeping up with table egg and processing demand. No unmanageable surpluses are reported at this date. Exact amounts vary from week to week.
10.	See answer to Part 3. Also CEMA now require that all surplus to table egg requirements owned by CEMA be sold for processing within 7 days.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as my first words, in light of some of the comments I made to my hon. friends immediately before the adjournment of this House last July, let me acknowledge that a funny thing happened to me in the course of my retirement from public life and I find myself, through a process which I cannot easily explain, diverted to the responsibilities of minister of finance. In taking over what I recognize is a heavy responsibility from my very able predecessor, the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner)-

speakeroldname: Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
-who faced with distinction a series of severe challenges in economic decisionmaking both at home and abroad, I have been bolstered by the expression of good wishes that I have received from all sides of this House and from across the country. I must confess that I would like to have had a little more time in which to learn the ropes. As it is, I have been undergoing an accelerated course of on-the-job training over the past several days during which other members of government and I have been considering, on an urgent basis, how best to deal with the developing economic problems confronting our country.
As underlined by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in speaking to the nation on television last night, and by the white paper which I have tabled in the House on behalf of the government, the powerful and deeply entrenched inflationary forces racking our economy now imperil our prospects for the future. We have reached the point where there is a very real danger that if inflation is not halted and reversed, it will grow to ever larger proportions, sapping our economic strength and undermining our prospects for resurgent growth of output, employment and the real income of Canadians.
In the government's judgment, there is now a critical need for the establishment of a concerted program of national action involving all governments and all Canadians to break the vicious spiral of cost and prices that endangers the stability of our economy and, indeed, of our whole society. What is equally important is that the strong public support so crucial to the success of such a national program also now exists for the first time in Canada.
Before outlining the broad approach being developed by the government for dealing immediately and over the longer term with the problems confronting us, I would like
Anti-Inflation
to try to put the origin and nature of these problems in some perspective. Over the course of the past three years, Canada, as a major trading nation and a major participant in international capital markets, has been heavily exposed to the enormous shocks that have reverberated throughout the world. We were buffeted first by immense inflationary pressures generated by soaring international prices for food, oil and industrial raw materials. As the world moved from runaway boom to the deepest and most prolonged recession of the post-war period, demand for many of our major exports plummeted, output was sharply cut back and unemployment sharply increased.
There is, of course, no possible way in which an economy such as ours could avoid being seriously affected by these adverse developments abroad. Throughout this period, however, government policy has had the consistent aim of doing everything that was practically possible to cushion the Canadian economy from the worst effects of these global shock waves. We formulated a number of measures aimed at doing what we could in Canada to get at the root of inflationary problems by increasing supply and by encouraging expansion of our productive capacity. At the same time, we brought forward a wide range of policies aimed at moderating the impact of inflation on the Canadian people through such means as substantial personal and commodity tax reductions, indexation of the personal income tax system and of family allowances, old age pensions and the Canada Pension Plan, and a wide range of subsidies to hold down the prices of certain basic foodstuffs and of petroleum. These measures served both to ease the burden of inflation on Canadians individually and to sustain the economy as a whole by preventing any serious erosion of real consumer income and expenditures.
We were among the first to take stimulative fiscal action to counter the adverse impact on our domestic economy of the impending recession that we foresaw developing abroad, although we in common with others underestimated the length and depth of that recession. Nevertheless, the expansionary fiscal policies introduced by the government, together with major programs that automatically come into effect to help stabilize the economy, such as the greatly expanded unemployment insurance system put in place a few years ago, have also played an important part in shielding Canadians from the worst effects of lagging growth and in sustaining the economy in the face of severe recession abroad.
All of these federal programs to cushion the impact of both inflation and recession, many of which have been complemented and reinforced by the provinces, have inevitably put heavy financial strains on both federal and provincial treasuries. But it has been the judgment of government generally that these measures were essential in both human and economic terms. They were essential to moderate the burden of sharply increasing prices and lack of jobs on individual Canadians, and essential to sustain the economy in order to prevent the build-up of massive unemployment because of the rapid growth of our labour force.
On the surface, our current economic position might appear to some Canadians as being reasonably favourable.

October 14, 1975
Anti-Inflation
Our economy has suffered a far less prolonged and severe recession than many other major industrial nations. Judged by such measures as the consumer price index or the price indexes of the goods we export and import, our rate of inflation would not appear to be out of line with the average for the industrial countries. The very large increase that has taken place in our current account deficit with other nations over the past several months can also be attributed in large measure to the fact that our economy has remained relatively strong, with the result that the pace of imports has considerably outstripped that of our exports.
Such considerations may be comforting, but they mask the reality of our situation. The hard fact is that the Canadian economy today is being subjected to underlying, domestically-generated inflationary forces that are far more severe than those being experienced by most of our major trading partners.
In no small measure, the deep-seated problem now plaguing us is a product of our very success in maintaining economic activity at a considerably higher level than that in most other industrial nations. Had we suffered as severe and prolonged an economic contraction as countries such as the United States, Germany and Japan, it is virtually certain that we would also have experienced substantially less build-up of cost pressures. But because we as a nation escaped the constraints forcefully imposed on other countries by severe recession and were not prepared to join together in exercising some agreed measure of selfrestraint, our underlying production costs have increased much more rapidly than those in countries such as the United States and Germany and still show no sign of decelerating significantly, as they do in Japan.
The real danger to our economy lies ahead. As countries like the United States, Germany and Japan pull out of their present deep recession, they can expect to enjoy very much higher productivity gains than Canada. The effect would be to widen substantially the differential between our unit costs and those of our major competitors.

Mr. Speaker, it is sometimes stressed that the threat to the competitive position of Canadian goods on domestic and foreign markets embodied in such measures can be offset by the depreciation of the Canadian dollar. Such a course brings but temporary relief. Dollar depreciation would simply increase the cost of imported goods and services, therefore intensifying inflationary pressures.
Dollar depreciation would bring but very limited and temporary relief to the more vulnerable areas of the Canadian economy, including our manufacturing industry whose competitive position may be more seriously affected by the so-called cost-push. But the basic reason is that continuous cost and price increases, coupled with constant erosion of our currency, offer no practical basis for a healthy and dynamic future economy. Such a course would intensify savings erosion, engulf money markets and hinder both the yield on new corporate investments and housing starts. These are the prime factors pointing to the necessity of controlling inflation in Canada.
[Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale).)
During these past years of economic upheaval, much time and effort has been fruitlessly spent in an effort to point the finger at one group or another as the prime source of all our troubles, with business, labour and governments all being singled out, at one time or another, as leading candidates for the villain's role. I think it would be truer to say that all of us have been caught up by the turbulent new forces which have gripped our economy, adjusting and responding as best we knew how to meet our respective needs and responsibilities. In the process, however, we have collectively tried to take out of the economy more than it has provided. In doing so we have created serious problems for the future. Notwithstanding some of the rhetoric, I think the vast majority of Canadians are convinced that the time has come when we must all pull back.
As the white paper makes clear, Mr. Speaker, the program formulated by the government for attacking the major problems facing the economy encompasses four different elements. These involve the maintenance of a balance of fiscal and monetary policies that will encourage economic recovery and at the same time provide for gradual moderation of inflation; limitations on the growth of government expenditures and the size of the public service; structural policies aimed at ensuring the necessary supplies of energy, food and housing, increasing the efficiency and competitiveness of the economy and bringing about an improvement in labour-management relations; and, finally, adoption of a prices and incomes policy.
Let me deal first with the latter program. I will have an opportunity, when implementing legislation is introduced for debate on second reading, to go more thoroughly into the details, so today I will confine myself to a brief outline. Tn the white paper, the government has proposed an initial set of broad guidelines to provide a measure of what it considers to be reasonable and responsible behaviour in the determination of prices, profits, rents, wages, salaries, dividends, fees, commissions and similar types of income. The government strongly urges that all Canadians adhere to the guidelines, which become effective today, both in the national interest and ultimately in their own interest.
Unless we can work together with a firm sense of national purpose, we shall all be the worse off. The success of this policy-or of any other form of incomes policy-depends vitally on the readiness of the great majority of the people to comply with it voluntarily. To ensure that the public interest prevails, however, the program will be reinforced by federal administrative machinery established to monitor price and income developments throughout the economy. This proposed new administrative arm, backed as an ultimate resort by the firm sanctions of the law, will, in particular, oversee compliance with the guidelines by the larger economic interests which play such a dominant role in the establishment of cost-price patterns across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, provincial governments whose contribution
will be essential to the success of the program are request-
October 14, 1975

ed to cooperate with the federal government by following the guidelines and ensuring that they are complied with by various provincial firms, organizations and communities. Besides doing everything they can to foster widespread support for that initiative among the general public, provinces are specifically requested to have rent increases and professional fees comply with those guidelines.
As I mentioned earlier, the legislation implementing the program as proposed by the government will provide the means of forcing top economic groups of Canada to comply with the guidelines. It will relate to firms or groups of related firms with over 500 employees and all construction companies with more than 20 employees as well as all those employed by those companies. Employees of groups of firms who will jointly negotiate agreements on an industrial scale will come within the provisions of that legislation as well as the firms which employ them. Professional individuals or firms will come under the provisions of the legislation. So will the federal government and every Crown corporation or other organization as well as their employees. Provincial governments, if they are willing to abide by those guidelines and have their organizations and municipalities comply with them will be free to do so or set up their own procedures. The legislation might also be applied to groups of seemingly vital importance for Canada through orders in council.

Mr. Speaker, the statutory provision will apply to somewhat more than 1,500 firms, roughly 5 per cent of the total number of firms in Canada. Approximately 2,300,000 employees of private sector firms will be covered, around two-thirds of the total number of employed persons in the private industrial sector of the economy. Approximately another 2,000,000 employees of all federal, provincial and municipal governments and agencies, hospitals and schools will also be covered if all public bodies in the provinces also participate, which would bring the total number of employees subject to the statutory guidelines to 4,300,000.
The agency primarily responsible for supervising the guidelines program will be the anti-inflation board, which will be appointed initially by order-in-council under the Inquiries Act prior to its establishment under the authority of the legislation. It will be responsible for providing such clarification of the guidelines as may be necessary, monitoring their observance and pinpointing actual or proposed increases in prices or incomes which appear to exceed those guidelines.
It is also being proposed to the provinces that a special public sector panel be established under the anti-inflation board to consider questions relating to prices and incomes involving governments and their agencies. We are suggesting that some members of this panel be nominated by provincial governments. One of the functions of the board will be to carry out discussions with all parties involved in an effort to bring about compliance with the guidelines. If the issue cannot be resolved satisfactorily, the board may refer it to the enforcement authority designated as the administrator and appointed by order-in-council, who may take appropriate action under the law to bring about com-
Anti-Inflation
pliance. Decisions of the administrator may be appealed within 60 days to the anti-inflation appeal tribunal which will also be established under the legislation. Decisions of the administrator may also be changed by direction of the governor in council. Decisions of the tribunal may, in turn, be appealed to the Federal Court of Appeal.
As a general principle, the guidelines provide that increases in prices undertaken by companies should be no more than the net increase in their costs. The way in which this principle applies, however, will depend on the nature and size of the enterprise and the kind of business in which it is engaged. Firms which are able to allocate costs to individual products are expected to increase their prices by no more than the actual increase in their costs for such products and to decrease prices if their costs are reduced. Firms which are unable to allocate costs to individual products are asked to establish price levels which would yield a pre-tax profit margin no higher than 95 per cent of its average profit margin over the last five fiscal years.
Different guidelines will apply to the distribution sector, which follows different pricing practices. As a general rule, retail and wholesale firms are expected not to increase customary mark-ups on various kinds of merchandise.
Banks and other financial institutions will be expected to follow the general rule, increasing service charges or interest rates only sufficiently to cover increases in their operating costs and other expenses, or increases in the interest rates which they pay for funds on deposit or borrowed.
As the House will appreciate, a difficult problem arises in the case of companies which sell a significant proportion of their output in the export market. As a general rule, such companies will be expected to sell abroad at the prevailing international market price, to sell in the domestic market at a price that is consistent with the guidelines, and to ensure that the Canadian market is fully supplied at that domestic price. Following discussions with those concerned, the government plans to impose a special levy in cases where the over-all profit margins of such companies exceed guideline limits. Prices received by farmers and fishermen on their products will be exempt from the guidelines. But we will be holding discussions with the provincial governments about the operations of agricultural marketing boards to ensure that their operations are consistent with the guidelines.
Turning to the question of incomes, the guidelines proposed will be governed by four main elements. The first is a basic protection factor which initially provides for income increases of 8 per cent in the first year of new contracts, 6 per cent in the second and 4 per cent in the third. The second factor provides for a further increase of 2 percentage points to take account of the long-term growth of productivity. For the average worker, therefore, the guidelines provide an increase in remuneration of 10 per cent. For employees who have fallen behind the increase in consumer prices over the past two or three years, the guidelines make provision for a catch-up increase of up to
29669 - 35

October 14, 1975
Anti-Inflation
2 per cent per year, bringing the maximum permissible increase to 12 per cent in the first year.
In the case of employees whose income over the past few years has risen by more than consumer prices, the permissible increase this year would be reduced by up to 2 percentage points, with the result that the maximum permissible gain would be no more than 8 per cent in the first year. In the event the actual increase in consumer prices exceeds the basic protection factor in one period, the permissible increases in a succeeding period would be raised so as to make it possible for the income of employees to keep pace with the rise in the cost of living.

Mr. Speaker, increases already granted are not affected by these guidelines. Also excluded will be agreements executed before the start of 1974 that have expired and are now being renegotiated.
The fourth point in the guidelines is the provision about minimum and maximum increases. At the lower end of the income ladder workers may get income increases up to $600 irrespective of the general guidelines. As to the upper income groups the ceiling for the average maximum increase is set at $2,400.
As I said earlier those guidelines would apply to those providing specialized services, and provincial governments are urged to use all their power to ensure the observation of those guidelines.
In that program the government intends to undertake intensive talks with the provinces as well as business, labour and other sectors. The guidelines set out in that policy statement were intended as "first" steps; we wanted thus to show that we are prepared to change certain things either following questions raised in Parliament or during the talks we are planning to have with all those concerned. We are entering a brand new area with which none of us are familiar; there will surely be difficulties and thorny issues. So it is important to maintain consultation and coordinate our efforts to solve the problems and difficulties that will come up.

The details involving the guidelines will be spelled out in regulations to be drawn up under the implementing legislation being submitted to parliament. In general terms, the guidelines are effective as of today, but the government recognizes that some uncertainty is bound to arise about their applications in a host of special circumstances. We will try to provide the necessary clarification as soon as possible. In the interval, particular care should be taken, especially by those subject to enforcement provisions, to ensure that any increases in prices or incomes are clearly within the intent of the guidelines. In this connection, I am hereby giving formal notice of intent that the guidelines to be established by regulation under the antiinflation act, when adopted by parliament, are applicable as of today.
No one should be under any illusion, Mr. Speaker, that
the prices and incomes policy we have proposed will bring
about any substantial reduction quickly in the inflation
that is so deeply embedded in our system. We have every reason to hope, however, that barring any new shocks from abroad it will serve to halt and gradually reverse the present spiral of costs and prices.
I should now like to deal with some of the broader questions that undoubtedly will be raised in connection with the prices and incomes program for which we are asking support from both parliament and the nation. It has been contended in some quarters, both inside and outside the House, that the government should have taken action long before now to establish some form of prices and incomes policy. There were others, of course, who argued equally as strongly against such a course, some of whom still continue to do so. In our view, the proposal for imposition of comprehensive, mandatory price and income controls that some urged on us 2 Vi years ago was very much the wrong policy at the wrong time. Such controls could not possibly have been effective in holding back the tidal wave of inflation sweeping over this country from abroad.

speechtext:
Such controls would also have been ineffective because in our judgment the strong public support essential to their success did not at that time exist. Indeed, the experience a few years ago in the United Kingdom, when determined opposition to controls brought the British economy to its knees, harshly demonstrated that controls can work very much against the interests of the economy if they are not firmly backed by the great majority of the people.
About a year ago it became apparent that the nature of the inflationary problem had begun to change, with the strongest inflationary pressures increasingly being generated at home rather than from abroad. The changing nature of the problem called for a changed response. Members will recall that the government devoted a great deal of time and effort over a period of several months in trying to reach agreement among various groups in our economy on a fair and equitable means of restraining increases in prices and incomes.
All groups recognized the severity of the problem posed by inflation, and we made considerable progress in developing a generally acceptable set of guidelines. Indeed, hon. members will recognize in the guidelines in the white paper the documents tabled by my predecessor in this House on May 8. In the end, however, we were unable to reach an understanding because of persistent doubt about whether the guidelines, if adopted, would in fact be observed.
Following the conclusion of our earlier efforts to secure an understanding on prices and incomes restraint, we were reluctant to contemplate some form of direct intervention by the government because there still remained some reason to hope that the spiral of costs and prices would
(Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale).
October 14, 1975

begin to abate, and because of our judgment that the necessary public support for such intervention did not exist. With each passing month it has become increasingly apparent that inflationary pressures have been intensifying rather than receding. It has become clear beyond any reasonable doubt, both to the government and to the great majority of Canadians, that it has now become absolutely essential to take decisive action to bring inflation under control.
The second major question that is bound to be debated is our intention of confining enforcement of the guidelines to the large economic groups within the economy, rather than establishing a comprehensive mandatory control system. We chose to follow this course because we wished to intervene as little as possible in the operations of the economy and in the lives of Canadians. We have sought to frame a selective system subject to enforcement that is flexible and reasonably manageable, one that will have the least adverse effect possible in distorting and disrupting the regular workings of our economy.
At the same time, we believe that the system we have proposed will be effective in achieving its purpose by ensuring the exercise of restraint by those groups which possess exceptional power to impose excessive price and income increases on other groups in the economy.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to touch briefly on the other elements that form part of the framework of policy required to strengthen the foundation of our economy. It is, of course, of critical importance that our fiscal and monetary policies be properly geared to maintain the economy on an even keel. In our judgment, the set of fiscal policies established in the June budget and the prevailing stance of monetary policy provide a reasonable balance in current economic circumstances. As we have learned from recent experience, however, economic circumstances can change swiftly and drastically. We are, therefore, very conscious of the need to stand ready to make changes in fiscal and monetary policies as they are required to respond to changing conditions.
During the past few years there has been a substantial increase in government expenditures, particularly at the federal level. As I suggested earlier, a very large part of this increase has been the consequence of measures adopted by governments to cushion the impact of both the sharply increased cost of living and of higher unemployment on Canadians, particularly those most adversely affected, and to offset the adverse effect on the economy as a whole of inflation and recession.
If we are to bring the underlying problem of inflation under control, however, it is now essential to do everything reasonably possible to restrain the further growth of government spending. In the budget last June, the government outlined substantial reductions that were being made in controllable expenditures in the current fiscal year to provide an offset for increases in outlays that could not be avoided either because of contractual or moral commitments or to meet requirements essential to the well-being of the economy and of the Canadian people.
Anti-Inflation
The substantial increase in government expenditures in recent years has unavoidably been accompanied by a substantial increase in the size of the public service. The June budget cut the projected growth for the current fiscal year from 4.1 per cent to 3.1 per cent. In the next fiscal year the increase in the federal public service will be restricted to 1.5 per cent. Essential increases in some areas will be largely offset by reductions in others, with the result that the majority of government departments will be permitted fewer man-years in 1976-77 than was the case in 1974-75. We believe that it should be the objective of all governments to limit the growth of public spending to the growth of gross national production. That will be our basic aim in the preparation of spending plans for the next fiscal year and the years beyond that.
The final element of the program relates to structural adjustments that need to be made in the economy to improve its capacity to provide certain essential supplies that we will require in future and to make our economic system more innovative, dynamic and efficient by reducing existing rigidities and intensifying competition.
The need to bring about a substantial reduction in the overall rate of inflation is made all the more pressing by the fact that certain relative price increases are unavoidable over time, increases that we can absorb without undue hardship if we can restore strong real growth of our national wealth. Phased increases in the price of energy, for example, are essential to meet the soaring cost of finding, developing and marketing the new energy sources that will be required in future to meet our needs for heat, light and power. Such increases are equally essential over time to promote more efficient use of our energy resources. In prevailing circumstances of much lower petroleum prices in Canada than abroad, it becomes all the more important to intensify other efforts to conserve energy consumption.
The substantially increased cost of housing must also be met if construction of the new residential units required for our growing population is to be undertaken. As the white paper stated, the federal government will shortly announce proposals for the provision of special new incentives to encourage increased housing construction. We will also be discussing with the provinces means of increasing the supply of serviced land for housing in order to put a damper on soaring land costs.
Higher prices for certain foods may also be unavoidable if farmers are to receive a return that is sufficient to cover their sharply rising costs and yield a fair and reasonable income to compensate for all their labours and investment. At the same time, however, we must also ensure that our price and marketing system are not structured to maintain inefficient agricultural production and distribution.
The government plans to bring forward at an early date the second phase of its policy to strengthen competitiveness of our economy, which is the surest guarantee of its efficient and effective operation. Together with provincial governments and other interested parties, we propose to scrutinize a wide variety of government policies and programs in an effort to find ways of reducing rigidities and costs that they may impose unnecessarily on various sectors of the economy.
