In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to underline one fundamental point, a point that is also emphasized in the white paper. Whatever differences of interest may exist between the various sectors that make up our economy are far outweighed by the common interest we all share in seeing that strong and stable growth of output, employment and the standard of living of Canadians is restored. It is, therefore, very much in the interest of every group to work together to achieve these national objectives.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
First, Mr. Speaker, with your permission, I would like to direct my comments to the new Minister of State (Mr. Marchand), previously Minister of Transport. I am sorry that he is not here today. Ten years ago, he decided to make the move to federal politics to reinforce national unity within confederation. With all his strength, he vigorously denounced separatism in Quebec. He also worked at making the two founding peoples of this country equal partners who now share fully in our national life. He accepted his heavy responsibilities with conviction, determination and courage. This man can be proud of his task and his work which was often thankless. The preoccupations and responsibilities of political life throughout the years have marked him and have affected his health. This led him to accept to play a less prominent role in the future. I had occasion to criticize the legislation that he defended and I have often doubted his administrative capacities.
Today, I wish to pay him a particular and personnal homage and to tell him that I respect him very profoundly and that I admire him sincerely. His fights throughout the years to defend certain fundamental principles put him in a very special class. I would like him to know that I have always shared the profound aspirations which have guided his political action. I hope that he will long stay with us and I wish him a very speedy recovery.
Mr. Speaker, our new Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has made quite a spectacular entrance into this job. I congratulate him on this appointment and I congratulate the new ministers, the switched ministers, the new parliamentary secretaries and the quiet-spoken new whip on the other side.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
I sincerely wish the new Minister of Finance well. I know he will appreciate that the doubts and concerns that I express today are something more than partisan in intent. I must say about him that he seems to be a quick learner. He has learned quickly from his predecessor, who has shown on more than one occasion that there are things worth lifting from time to time from this side of the House.
[Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale).J

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: I will miss some of the stellar performances of the former minister of finance. As he is probably aware, I have been inviting him to schedule a further performance at the earliest opportunity. I do not know whether we are going to hear from him in the course of the day, but I understand there are already some who thought that perhaps the minister had resigned because he felt the government was not tough enough and who have, since last evening, begun to wonder whether the former minister of finance resigned because he thought the government has gone too far and is too tough, particularly in view of some of the scathing things which the former minister of finance said from time to time about compulsory price and wage controls. I look to the minister to clarify his position at the very earliest opportunity.

speakeroldname: Mr. Broadbent:
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: You can wait.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: There are some unpleasant things which have to be said today about the record of this government and the process by which it has come to the point of presenting this white paper today. I want to assure the House and the people in Canada that today and in the days ahead as this new program unfolds, my observations and criticisms are, and will be, directed toward making the government work to help make our society work. Some might think that this is an occasion of pretty substantial vindication of my party and myself.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Personally, I do not take very much pleasure in that. I have been vindicated so many times before that I do not take much pleasure from it now, not because I do not enjoy being vindicated, not because I dislike it, but because I believe that the reluctant and belated confirmation of a diagnosis does not necessarily ensure that the real cure is on the way. I would feel very much better if the medical staff on the case had a far better record.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: I am relieved by the fact that the government is finally doing something, but I remain concerned that it has taken so long to take any kind of action, and I am, quite frankly, very dubious about the government's fundamental sincerity. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), on television and here in the House, has done very little so far to purge me of my doubts. I say very bluntly to you, sir-and I have to say this-that I believe very little of what this government says.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
I say that this government's biggest challenge in getting any program off the ground is to get Canadians to believe what it says. If the government is going into this endeavour under the impression that its credibility is high, and that by and large things will sort of come together, if it shows us the kind of cavalier behaviour which it has adopted so many times in the past, this country will be headed for literally terrible consequences, because the official opposition in this House has no monopoly on doubt and suspicion with regard to this
October 14, 1975

government or with regard to this government's program. Those who have been suffering the most will question why the government has waited until those who are best able to look after themselves have done so by and large. Those who have lost ground, particularly those who have lost jobs, will wonder how far off renewed opportunities are for them, and whether catching up will ever be a realistic prospect for them.
Trust and confidence have been injured in our society. There are difficult times ahead for our economy. They will not be quickly or easily healed. They will not be healed at all if the government appears to be less than frank or less than fair-minded as it proceeds with this endeavour. No amount of bureaucracy and no exercise of power will be any substitute for frankness, openness and exemplary conduct on the part of this government. If that is not forthcoming, then the whole exercise will do nothing more than compound the injury that has already been done-and that would indeed be tragic.
The government comes to the House today and seeks support for its general outline of this program. There is no vote involved, just the assessment and comments which will be put forward in the course of today's debate. So far as the white paper is concerned, it is a pretty superficial treatment of what is a very complex matter. But I will not be critical about that today; I simply say that the white paper obviously raises far more questions than it answers-and you can be sure that I am familiar with the questions involved because I have probably been asked more questions on this than anybody else in the country: I am perhaps still the ranking expert in terms of questions about this matter.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
There is legislation to come in the next days and weeks. This House will be dealing in greater detail with the substance of this program, perhaps piece by piece or perhaps all together: we do not know today. Today I will not attempt to go into detail. Rather, I want briefly to deal with the recent history in the present context of this move by the government. Earlier I said that I could believe very little of what this government says, and that, sir, is just another example of my gift for understatement.
I am prepared to concede that the government may not face quite the degree of difficulty in getting some of what it says believed in the country at large as it will have in getting me to believe it, because the country at large has not sat here in the House in my seat for eight years watching "Cynicism Incorporated." The country at large was not here following the 1972 election when the former minister of finance surfaced after an election, implementing measures which he had said during the campaign would bankrupt the country. There was a modest increase in old age pensions, some needed tax cuts and, of course, tax indexing. It was quite a turn-around show following the election of 1972. It was quite a show indeed, if one likes that sort of thing. It was slick, smooth and totally devoid of principle.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
Anti-Inflation

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
In some judgments, that sort of thing is nothing more than clever politics. In my book, judgments of that nature are just as shallow as the acts themselves. I do not want to make myself out to be qualified to moralize, but I do believe that a great part of the problem of distrust which runs through our society today has been created by overdoses of that kind of politics and those kinds of judgments.
When we get right down to it, we are really dealing with a moral issue in what is before us. I am sure the Prime Minister realizes this, but I am not sure that he and his government recognize that they have to come to grips with it in their own behaviour. I know that the economic and social objectives will not be met unless there is some confidence abroad that the Prime Minister and the government are coming to grips with this issue and the fact that they are not an exception to the moral principles with which we are dealing.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
This is an unspoken component of leadership which will have a great bearing on the success or failure of the government's initiative of intervention which is outlined in this white paper, and it cannot be a "sometime" thing, if there is to be any change of bringing this country together in a shared, sincere attempt to improve conditions in our society.
Here, again, I say that this government in its recent record does not inspire my confidence. The way the announcement of this program was handled was disturbingly reminiscent to me of the kind of thing we saw when the crunch was on in the petroleum crisis. When that finally hit home to the Prime Minister and his colleagues, despite years of forewarning, they put on a great act at having been taken by surprise. Then there was a flurry of activity and exhortations and the Prime Minister went on television and solemnly said a few things. It was a very impressive drama.
Today, we are evidently right back where we started, again living in a fool's paradise as far as energy policy and practices are concerned. The minister touched on energy policy this afternoon. Where is the vaunted conservation program which was to emerge from that crisis? Where are the benefit-sharing arrangements with the Atlantic provinces and Quebec? Where is the adequate research program on alternate sources of energy? Today, those Canadians who can afford to are wasting just as much energy as ever. The government has not followed through on its own initiative and what was alleged to be leadership at that time.
After his television appearance on that occasion, the Prime Minister virtually dropped from public view. Are we going to see the same thing happen this time? The then minister of energy, mines and resources-who is on the hot seat again today-was front and centre on television, promoting the distribution of a booklet which did not even exist at that time, a booklet supposedly being produced by a conservation office which took ages to staff.
Rising prices have constituted the only actual incentive to energy conservation we have seen in this country. Con-

October 14, 1975
Anti-Inflation
servation is being practised by those who cannot afford not to practise it. The white paper essentially acknowledges that. This is certainly not providing leadership by example. On the contrary, as far as this government is concerned, if one wants to see an example of perverse construction for the Canadian climate one does not have to look any farther than two blocks west, at the new Bank of Canada building.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
The limousines roll on; ministerial car pools have faded away like mentions of the just society. Conservation is demonstrably an endangered species within the confines of the operations of this government. Wasteful trappings for show have been the rule rather than the exception. If the Prime Minister and his colleagues hope to have any real chance of being taken seriously this time around with this general restraint program, they had better quickly show Canadians that they can mend their own ways as far as energy policy is concerned.
I say to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of Finance, "Don't try to snow us. Show us."

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
I understand that the Prime Minister will be speaking in this debate. I do not know whether I will hear him or not, because I made a commitment to accept a dinner engagement with Dr. Kissinger-another great man-but I will read what the Prime Minister has to say if I should, regretfully, miss hearing him in this debate. I hope he will take the opportunity to deal with some of the fears, doubts and suspicions which his record, more than anything else, has raised.
The energy area is not the only recent example of the Prime Minister's starting something off with a good deal of flair, and then appearing to have tired of it and abandoning the whole thing. This was true, for example, in the consensus exercise to which the Minister of Finance referred today. Early in that game the Prime Minister gave assurances to the House that he accepted the top level responsibility for that program. He certainly did nothing to alter the widespread presumptions that he would remain very personally involved in it, using the weight of his office and the strength of his talents to bring it all off.
Whether this was what the Prime Minister intended the perception to be, this is in fact what the perception was and the Prime Minister must surely have been aware of that. It subsequently appeared that he withdrew from participation in that program. This was when I began to be convinced that the whole consensus operation was a sham. The Prime Minister may recall that my colleagues and I started out prepared to support that effort as we understood it in its broad terms. In that case we never got beyond broad terms, and the Prime Minister never appeared to go beyond the very short term as far as involvement was concerned, so we ended up with nothing that deserved support. As it turned out, we were not alone in that view when the last act hit the stage.
Now we are looking at a program which involves much bigger stakes and the same kind of presumptions have already been made about the involvement of the Prime Minister as were made when the so-called consensus exer-

cise began. If those presumptions are in error, the Prime Minister might as well tell us so today. If the presumptions are well founded, he should let us know as much as he can about the planned extent of his own involvement in this general restraint program in the coming months. Let there be no nonsense or kidding ourselves with regard to this matter. The Prime Minister has conditioned the country to a personal style of administration. I mean no slight to the Minister of Finance or any other minister in the government when I say that there is no question about who runs the government: it is the Prime Minister. The kind of effort which he put into the 1974 election campaign is the kind of effort he will have to make not only to launch this general restraints program but to sustain it, fortify it and reinforce it in the months ahead. That is absolutely essential. It is, also, absolutely essential that the Prime Minister should quickly get over any indigestion he may suffer in having swallowed himself in the course of announcing this program.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
There is really no room in this exercise for integrated rationalization, revisions of history, stretches of imagination or preoccupation with trying to grasp straws in self-justification. We heard the new Minister of Finance go through this whole thing again here this afternoon. This is a program of general, large-scale mandatory price and income controls and it is going to be tough enough to live with knowing what it is, without the Prime Minister contorting himself to say that it is not what it is.
Let me say this. We have said for some time that an anti-inflationary program must be comprehensive, that a program of controls, short-term controls, has a certain role to play, but they have to be reinforced with other measures which include appropriate fiscal and monetary policy. The Minister of Finance touched on this briefly today.
I read a sentence in the white paper which I wish I had had more time, in the course of a busy day, to try to figure out. Perhaps if I read it here, the Prime Minister can explain later exactly what it means. The passage says that the federal government shares the view that the trend of total spending by all governments in Canada should not rise more quickly than the trend of the gross national product. What does that mean, Mr. Speaker?

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: It is trendy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
It may be trendy; but if I ever read a weasel sentence, that is it. I think it must have been written by the Department of Justice.
Furthermore, we have insisted that any such program must be equitable and it must be seen to be equitable. That is why I am pleased that the Prime Minister gave the assurance that ministers of the Crown and all the rest of us in this House would be kept within the general guidelines even though technically, because of some statutory arrangement, we might have been able to avoid the guidelines. This is very important.
The only other specific aspect of the program that I wish to refer to today is the duration, because in the course of
October 14, 1975

considering the bill we will be looking at the equity of the various proposals, some of which are concerning the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) and others of which are concerning some of my colleagues. We will have an opportunity, when the bill is before the House, to consider these specifics in detail.
I want to speak briefly today about the duration of the program, because member after member on the other side of the House, and minister after minister-including the Prime Minister-have kept on saying that even if mandatory price and income controls are accepted by the public, they will not get at the root cause of inflation; any benefit that they might achieve is of short-term duration. They have said this so often that they must say it in their sleep. I, personally, advocated short-term controls during 1973 and 1974, particularly during the election campaign, because I believed, in the circumstances which existed, that short-term, general controls on prices and incomes for a period of roughly 18 to 24 months could break the inflationary expectations that existed and could provide a framework which would enable us to fight inflation on a long-term basis, and a framework, also, within which we could continue to expand our economy and fight regional disparities.
I put it forward on this short-term basis. I emphasized at that time, as I have throughout most of my adult life, that I am opposed to long-term, comprehensive controls on prices and incomes because it is very clear this would lead to a different kind of economy than we have; that long-term controls would lead to a high degree of centralization of power and control in the hands of a few officials in Ottawa. That is not the kind of Canada I want to see, and I do not think it is the kind most Canadians want to see. I do not want to be a party to bringing it about. Yet the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and all the others who not only a year ago, but since then, ridiculed short-term controls and ridiculed this whole procedure as having, at best, very short-term benefits, are not putting before the House a program that goes beyond short-term controls. One would have to say these are controls of medium term, in terms of durability. It is nonsense for anybody to suggest these are different because they are voluntary. They are not voluntary; they are compulsory.
I hope that if the Prime Minister and the government persist in this "long-term" kind of talk, persist in seeking authority for these long-term controls of at least twice the duration of the sort of thing my party had in mind, they will at least be prepared to make provision for a parliamentary review of the controls and how they are working, providing an opportunity of parliamentary recall, say at the end of 18 months or two years. I just cannot understand how a Prime Minister and ministers who ridiculed the possible benefits of short-term controls, and exaggerated the dangers of those short-term controls, can now come before this House and, to use a very common and perhaps vulgar expression, have the gall to ask this parliament to delegate to a board and the governor in council these extensive powers lasting over a very substantial period of time.
Anti-Inflation
These are not voluntary controls. What is to be gained by the Prime Minister going on television and trying to have this thing both ways; trying to say, "We are acting. We are doing things firmly and, after all, it is only voluntary and we are only interfering with a few people"? That is an insult to the intelligence of Canadians.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: It is a bad start. This is essentially, in principle and in practice, the kind of program that the government said a year ago, and has been saying many times since then, would not work. The government said that kind of program would not work and had not worked anywhere; that it had been tried elsewhere but would not be accepted by Canadians. Let there be no doubt about it; this is exactly the kind of program the government said would never work anywhere and would not be accepted by Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Wagner:
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: That's Liberal morality.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Anyone who says this is a different kind of program should look at the questions and answers contained in the transcripts of 20 or 30 of my 1974 election news conferences.
I say to the government, do not persist in these silly games. Semantics designed to fit the square peg of infallibility into the round hole of reality will not get anyone anywhere. I say to the government, do not waste everybody's time and do not further try everybody's patience. The government won the election with means they must live with, but they will not win the present battle against Canada's tremendous economic problems with anything less than honesty with the Canadian people.
I will not be around here much longer in my present capacity to rub the government's nose in it, so why not play it straight and give this program a better chance of success than the government has given it by indulging in all this pretence? The government is under the duty to play it straight for a change. Just look at how the government allowed things to drift in the last 15 months since the election while it tried to stall off the inevitable, or at least buy time for a decent interval before swallowing itself. That precious time was unconscionably wasted and cannot be recovered.
Over the course of that time, things got more and more out of hand. A week before the resignation of the former minister of finance, the Bank of Canada announced a substantial increase, from 8.25 per cent to 9 per cent, in the bank rate. The Bank of Canada's actions are, of course, determined in the context of the general economic policies of this country's government. The Bank of Canada does not operate as a thing unto itself. I was dismayed by its action, particularly as a maritimer.
Speaking in the absence of any explanation by anyone in the cabinet, the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Bouey, later addressed the annual meeting of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. What he said boiled down to three

October 14, 1975
Anti-Inflation
things: first, deepening inflation in Canada is a very critical problem and it is not being taken seriously enough; second, the Bank of Canada's duty is to safeguard the integrity of the Canadian dollar in a psychological climate where the value and stability of money itself is not trusted; third, the continuing drift must be halted and reversed at virtually any cost in terms of unemployment and hardship. He said we cannot have any realistic hope of achieving sustained economic growth in the long run unless we bring inflation under control. The governor's words and the Bank of Canada's actions constitute a clear condemnation of the inaction of the government for more than one year following the attainment of its mandate for leadership in the 1974 election; and it is not as if no one had warned the government that it had better take humane and sensible action much earlier.
Throughout 1973 and up to and through the 1974 election campaign, we stressed that a priority objective of the program we were proposing was the encouragement of growth and the improvement of employment prospects in the country. As I said earlier in the context of suggesting a program to fight inflation, that could have been accomplished if the government had had the guts and heart to seize its responsibilities in 1974. We said that productivity and jobs could be pursued in a climate of stability if quick and comprehensive action was taken. We said that with conditions as they were, a move to achieve stability and maintain orderly growth was worth the price of a temporary intervention program. But now, Madam Speaker, in the autumn of 1975, we face the worst of both worlds- widespread and prolonged intervention and another massive economic slowdown.
It is said that justice delayed is justice denied. The acceptance of responsibility too long delayed has led to irresponsibility through default. The government diddled and dawdled along and let things get so far out of hand that we are mired where we are today. The Minister of Finance need not try to persuade me that this country's economic conditions require action by this government. I do not know who he thinks he is talking about when he speaks of people who think conditions in this country look pretty good. He must be far up some ivory tower. The less prosperous parts of our country are in for another pounding. Small business will again be hit most severely. The new Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) knows that as well as I do. He knows, as I do, the disastrous effects of harsh monetary policy on his part of the country and mine. The Atlantic provinces have been through all this before, as have other areas of slow growth of this country. They are the first to feel the effects and the last to recover from the damage, damage which offsets federal help through DREE assistance.
If the government wants co-operation in its effort, let it deal frankly and with some humility with this aspect of its economic policy. The word "voluntary" is meaningless in this context. What is voluntary about a small businessman's reaction to sky-high interest rates? He either pays them and stays afloat a little longer, or he does not pay them and goes under right away. Let us not have any more weasel-words from the other side of the House. Let us have
a frank admission from the Prime Minister about the government's contribution to our problems. Since 1968, his government has been a major force in both eroding the value of the Canadian dollar and raising the cost of borrowing. The Prime Minister talks about people demanding too much from the economy Let him take a good look at what his government has demanded from our economy, and let him tell the House why he chose to make campaign promises last year worth between $3 billion and $4 billion. What does he think about that now?
The government's approach to restraint in its June budget was another outright sham-transparently so. Not many were prepared to take it as a serious demonstration of leadership by example. That is the record to date. That is the pattern which the government has shown the country, with the Prime Minister occasionally popping up on television at some dramatic moment. This is the record and this is the pattern. This is what the Prime Minister and his government have to overcome if they are to have any chance at all of making a go of what they have announced.
My party is in the position, today, of extending support to the general intentions of this program as expressed in the white paper before us. Quite simply, common sense and the welfare of the country demand that we do. We do not at this time go beyond that. Any support for the actions of the government in the days ahead will have to be earned, and judgments on that score will be governed by the factors I have outlined.
I am pleased to be able to say, without immodesty, Madam Speaker, that my party has honestly tried to fulfil its own obligation to Canadians. We have dealt frankly and openly with the country and we will continue to do so. Whatever this may have cost us politically would not begin to measure up to the cost to our country if, from this point forward, the government fails to do so.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Edward Broadbent (Oshawa-Whitby):
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Madam Speaker, before I deal directly with the subject matter for debate this afternoon, I wish to join the colleagues of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) in expressing my personal admiration for the very exceptional job the leader of the Conservative party did for his party on the question of intellectual, moral and political integrity in the 1974 election campaign.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Broadbent:
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: I am sincere when I say that there are times in politics when losers contribute much more to the image of a politician than do winners.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Broadbent:
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Although we had very serious disagreements with the policy of wage and price controls that were argued for at the time of the 1974 election campaign by the leader of the Conservative party, as indeed did many of his supporters, I have been told on good authority-perhaps this is not known-that during the early stages of that campaign some Conservative members had done a survey and found out that the issue was not popular. There was real concern that perhaps they should shift ground and abandon the policy in mid-campaign. Certain political parties in this country, and certain political leaders, would not be above doing precisely that.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakeroldname: Mr. Broadbent:
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: I am told that the immediate, serious and sober response to that suggestion by the Conservative party's leader was that he would have none of it; that he was committed to the program, he believed in it and would stick with it. That kind of political leadership is something that democratic societies frequently lack. It is something to which his colleagues were paying tribute today, and I join them in that tribute.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Broadbent:

Turning more directly to the subject at hand, the opposite kind of attitude has been conveyed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). In 1974, the Prime Minister went to the people of Canada with a whole series of promises. He did not do that in 1968. At that time he had a sort of playboy image, the politician who liked to smile and dance. That was such a bizarre experience for Canadians that they voted for him in very substantial numbers. In 1972, he campaigned as a philosopher king. He did not want to talk about such mundane matters as housing, the cost of living and unemployment. He was almost defeated. Perhaps he and his government should have been defeated in 1972.

speakeroldname: Mr. Broadbent:
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM

In 1974, he went to the country with a good program, a program which very many people took seriously; the people seriously believed in it. He made categorical promises for the first time. He said we could expect a new urban policy involving financial assistance of various kinds, including funds for rapid transit development. He promised a new transportation policy which would redress the legitimate grievances of western Canadians with regard to freight rates. He undertook to deal with the freight rate structure and give Canada an over-all transportation policy. Nothing whatever has been done about that, either.
Then, again, just before the election he admitted in Vancouver that there was a housing crisis-those were his words-and led us to believe that something would be done about it. But nothing has been done. He told us during the 1974 campaign that he was concerned about the degree of foreign ownership and he made a commitment that 50 per cent of investment in the resource sector from that time on would be Canadian. As we saw when we got part II of the foreign investment review legislation at the end of the summer, that idea also went out of the window. Virtually every policy he had been talking about

urban policy, transportation, housing, foreign ownership-all the great promises of the 1974 campaign have been cynically dismissed.
The Liberals, above all, claim they can give the country economic leadership. This was the basis upon which they challenged the Conservative party. They were critical of the proposal of prices and incomes control put forward by the Leader of the Opposition. It is true that we shared in that criticism. But the main contention of the Prime Minister and his colleagues was that they alone could really manage the Canadian economy. However, what has happened in terms of economic leadership generally?
Bear in mind that we in Canada enjoy many advantages which are not common to all industrial countries. We have important natural resources at our disposal, unlike a number of western industrialized countries. We possess sufficient sources of energy to supply our industrial machine. We are able to call upon a well educated and well trained labour force. In short, we enjoy advantages which would have enabled us to make a real impact in terms of economic recovery in the last year and a half if only we had had a government willing to show economic leadership. But we have not had such a government. In the 18 months since the election, unemployment has risen; it has not gone down. The cost of living has gone up, not down as the Prime Minister promised; it has been increasing at the rate of 11 per cent. Housing starts have consistently declined. Mortgage interest rates have consistently gone up, not down as they should.

In terms of economic growth, the last six quarters in the period since the election have shown negative results, stagnation in every quarter of the six except one, and in that quarter I believe the growth rate was one-quarter of one per cent. That is the measure of economic leadership which members opposite have provided. That is what the management team on the other side-that gifted group, as they like to think of themselves as being-managed to do with the best trained labour force and the best situation when it comes to natural resources that one could imagine.
As to the speech which the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) read a short while ago, it might just as easily have been read by his successor. I do not blame the hon. gentleman directly; his speechwriters prepared the text. The point is that when it speaks of the government's economic performance, it still does so in self-congratulatory terms. Instead of coming here and saying, "We have made serious mistakes; various things have gone wrong; certain policies did not turn out to be the right ones, and we therefore intend to change things," the Liberals never admit they do anything wrong. They say, "We are still doing better than anybody else, but for some peculiar reason, despite how well we have done, we are now going to turn through 180 degrees."

speakeroldname: Mr. Broadbent:
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Turning to the program which has been put forward today, I intend to deal with it in terms of five specific criticisms. I wish to make it clear, though, that our party does not accept the view that the most acute economic problem we have to deal with now is inflation. We agree that inflation is a matter of very serious concern and that it has to be dealt with, but we are very disturbed to see a white paper presented to us today which has been described as merely an attack on inflation rather than as a package intended to deal with both inflation and unemployment.
After all, this is a country with one of the highest levels of persistent unemployment in the industrialized world- over 700,000 of our people are currently out of work-and it should surely be the concern of the government to deal with unemployment as well as inflation. So, while I intend to concentrate my criticism on the anti-inflation program, let me say that we in our party do not in any way agree with the government that the overwhelming attention it is directing to the issue of inflation is the proper position to have taken.
First, I want to deal with the proposal for price control which the government has introduced. There is a claim that the procedure to be followed will, in itself, be sufficient for full control over prices to be realized. In the view of our party, this is simply not the case. I intend to outline the way in which the government proposes to operate, if I understand its intentions correctly, and then go on to suggest reasons why we do not feel its proposals will work.
We are told that firms able to allocate costs to individual products will, in principle, be required to maintain a constant per unit profit level in dollar terms. Firms which are unable to allocate costs to individual products will be assessed on a total profit basis; they will, in principle, be required to hold down their percentage pre-tax net profit
[Mr. Broadbent.1
margin to a level no greater than 95 per cent of the last five-year average.
For firms engaged in distribution at the retail and wholesale levels, the profit guideline is based on gross profit margins-profit as a percentage of sales. Let us not be misled by the rather technical language which is being used here. In our view, this is not enforceable as a price control mechanism, whatever side benefits it might have. First of all, if these guidelines are to be enforced in any effective way, an army of bureaucrats will be required far in excess of the resources which the government is apparently willing to commit to this exercise. We are not in favour of hiring a lot of bureaucrats, but we say that if you are going to enforce this kind of proposal you must hire many more people than the 500 which is the figure I have heard used in respect of the number the government plans to hire, or otherwise you will not have the people to do the checking.
Secondly, in our view the companies concerned will have virtually unlimited opportunities to use their high-priced accountants and clever corporation lawyers to manipulate their books and pad their costs in ways which will allow them to circumvent the intent of the guidelines. This is a crucial point. In this sense I do not question the honesty of the corporations. I am saying that if you have a law which depends for its enforcement on the determination of certain profit levels and it is to the advantage of a corporation to see profit levels in a different way, you can be sure it will look for every conceivable and legal way of getting around these guidelines by redefining its profits.
We in this party are convinced that the experience of other countries would indicate that not only have corporations been able to get around such mechanisms, there, but we can fully expect them to do so here.
Thirdly, the government makes it clear that retailers and wholesalers will be permitted to raise prices of individual products without hinderances, subject only to the condition that should the board decide some day to make an inquiry into their operations, the particular retailer or wholesaler involved would only have to demonstrate that its total profits were within the guidelines.
Firms are expected to refrain from increasing the price of a product more frequently than once every three months, except where this would impose a hardship on the firm, in addition to which, and I quote from page 17 of the white paper, "Retailers and wholesalers will be exempt from this requirement". They are not going to be required to abide by the general rule, which is a crucial one, in terms of enforcement of price control mechanisms of this kind.
Fourthly, the white paper says that firms will be allowed to exceed the profit guidelines if the excess profit results from "unusual productivity gains resulting from the efforts of the firm, or of favourable cost developments". That is found on page 19 of the white paper.
What does that mean? That refers to any kind of innovative technique for increasing profit-making capacity
October 14, 1975

which, during the productive stage of an activity, will enable the firm to get whatever profits it can, or attain whatever level of profit the market will bear. If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) thinks I am wrong in that statement I would like him to correct me. That certainly is my interpretation of it. As long as this condition is met the profits of a company are unlimited, and if profits are unlimited then we do not have effective price controls through a profit control mechanism because profit control goes right out the window.
For those four reasons, briefly stated, and I am not going to labour them for rhetorical or for any other purposes, we hope the Minister of Finance during the question period, or another minister when makin j a speech during the debate, will deal with them. We simply believe that the guidelines will be totally ineffective whatever the government's good intentions might be. I am prepared to admit that we must take the legislation at its face value and assume the government is serious about it. Whatever the government's intention, there is not going to be effective price control through the profit control mechanism.
I want to deal with the efficacy of the board set up to enforce the provisions, particularly in view of the announcement today that the Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin and Beryl Plumptre have been appointed to key positions.
Let me say at the outset that Jean-Luc Pepin, when he was a member of this House, was a man who in personal terms I enjoyed and admired greatly. I want to add immediately that in terms of his own policy and political orientation he is precisely the kind of man who should not be given the job he has been handed. What has he done since he left the government? He is now a senior officer in the Power Corporation. He has been very much involved in developing a trading business for Canada. This is laudable, and I am not questioning his business objective or his intention there. There is nothing wrong with that if that is the kind of goal you want to pursue. What is wrong is to put him in charge of this kind of an agency which is intended to protect the consumer, because he is a man whose whole orientation has been on the other side of the ledger. This is analagous, no more and no less, to putting-

I was going to use a different analogy, but the Prime Minister has given an entirely appropriate one. It is analogous to putting a fox in with the chickens. Perhaps now that he recognizes that point he will reconsider this appointment.
As for Beryl Plumptre-well, dear old Beryl, ever since she has headed the Prices Review Board, has been struggling vigorously and consistently with infinite determination to find a case of excess profits. For some strange reason she has never succeeded. With all the investigations she has conducted on behalf of the Food Prices Review Board she has never found one case of excess profits. So Canadians can really rest assured knowing that Jean-Luc Pepin and Beryl Plumptre are in charge! They can go to sleep at night with total confidence that when they get up in the morning prices will be just and corporations will be sitting back taking lower profits, and the ship of state is in good hands. Well, I do not think so, Madam Speaker. I do
Anti-Inflation
not think the appointments were appropriate. I think they are such that they will encourage Canadians to view with little optimism the efficacy of a board being set up to administer and apply regulations which, as I have already said, on their own are shaky indeed.
Therefore I conclude on behalf of my party that the prices control mechanism in this set of proposals is a sham or a hoax, and whatever its purpose or its intent the result will not be price control.
The one element of the package we do think will be effective is the salary and wage control proposal. It may not surprise some people that this accounts for the fact that every businessman I saw interviewed about the proposals seemed to think they were good. This might have something to do with the fact that they now know their employees' wages will be effectively controlled. These controls will affect the hourly-rated employee and the person on a weekly salary basis who has none of the special opportunities of other people, and I will come to this in a moment, to get around the controls. They will have their wages restricted. There is no question but that on the one hand the prices control mechanism will be ineffective and on the other hand the wage and salary control mechanism will be totally effective.
I suspect this is what the Minister of Finance had in mind when he said in a loose moment to members of the press that when he saw the proposals he found them frightening. I assume he was speaking on behalf of the average worker in Canada at that time. These proposals will not be frightening, and I say this quite seriously, to most professional people.
Whatever the government tries to do in terms of law, and I am sure it will try to plug the loopholes, it has set the guidelines to apply to the fees of the professional people and not to their incomes, and this is on the theory that it does not want to discourage the initiative to work. So, if one worked longer hours one would receive more pay. I agree with that. It should apply to the fees and not to the income.
The point I want to make is that no matter how you come down with emphasis, it will not be operational for the upper income professional people because they can get around it. This would involve most lawyers. There are a few honest lawyers in this country. My colleague wants me to name them. I shall not do that. As we know, most lawyers work on sort of a percentage basis for business clients. They vary their fee according to the particular amount of money involved in a project. How will the incomes of those lawyers be controlled? They will not be in the same position as the auto worker, the bus driver, or the secretary. The lawyer will get around it. If an architect should have a particularly complex project then he makes a judgment. Without questioning his honesty I suggest he says it is more complex than another project, and up goes his fee. That will not be challenged.
Virtually all professionals working in the private sector will be able to get around these controls. This means that unfairness is built right into this program at the outset.

Apart from that type of unfairness we have the figures selected by the minister of $600 and $2,400. Already I have had calls from people who expect to receive the $600 and who believe it somehow is guaranteed. Of course that is not the case. A misunderstanding exists in that regard. This is a maximum figure in respect of those on low incomes. The most one may receive if he should be on the minimum wage scale would be an increase of $600 under the guidelines.

If I have misinterpreted this then I hope the error will be pointed out, now or later. However, as I understand it, the 10 per cent means that if one's income is $6,000 the most such a person could receive would be 10 per cent of that, which is $600. I do not know where the error is. The Prime Minister was shaking his head. I will look to him to correct this later.
Because most low-income people are not in trade unions and do not have a strong bargaining agency not only are they unlikely to get the $600 but, on the contrary, virtually 90 per cent of them will not come near it because there is no mechanism to ensure that they will receive that money. Did the government at least bring in a minimum program for these people to make sure they receive this? No. Did it change its federal minimum income wage law upwards somewhat so that these people would receive it? No. It said to the poor people of Canada who are at the bottom end of the scale in terms of income and who do not have a trade union, "too bad". That is what will happen in their case. They will not get the $600. The point we make on that issue is that it should have been made very clear to Canadians that they will not receive this as a right, and that most likely those down at that end of the scale will not receive it at all.
The second point we make in that connection is that the $600 level should be raised. Surely the $600 figure is too low. It is at the bottom end of the scale. How high it should be raised is a question on which I do not presume to give a definitive answer, but it must be substantially above that $600 level. The range is too great in terms of the $600 and the $2,400. The bottom amount simply is too low for people in Canada already living at the poverty level where they will remain in the years ahead.
The third point I make is that pensioners in Canada are not getting anything. One would have thought that a program dealing with inflation would deal with that category of people who are out of the labour market, who are not able to cope and who are dependent now, as has been mentioned, on an indexed pension. That is the situation for most pensioners in Canada unless they live in a province such as British Columbia or a couple of others, not necessarily provinces with NDP governments, which have taken additional steps to bring their incomes up above the poverty level. The point is that even with the indexed pension the level is still too low.
If the government wanted to deal with one category of person requiring some additional outlay of capital now,
(Mr. Broadbent.]
surely it should have been the pensioner, but there is nothing at all in this program for pensioners.
Then there is the matter of housing. If one thinks of the inflation which has been troubling Canadians in a serious way in the last couple of years, housing is one of the main issues. Surely the government should have done something on the supply side in a very significant proportion, to deal with the housing situation. It brought forward the idea at the federal level of rent control, which we have argued for and which we support in that part of the program. However, I say that unless the rent control program is complemented in the most serious way by a program to increase the supply of housing very significantly in the next year or two, it in itself would simply lead to horrendous headaches in a short period of time. You cannot have one without the other. If you have rent control, you must also have an imaginative and expansionary program to increase the supply of housing. There is nothing in the white paper to indicate this.
There is in the white paper a reference to some changes in the housing legislation but I suggest, given the record of this government which has not been reticent about patting itself on the back in the past inappropriately, that if we are to see a significant departure in respect of the housing program we would have seen those words in the white paper. One would have seen that there is to be a new major housing thrust or significant development, but that is not there. All that is indicated is that there will be some modification in the housing legislation. That, for our party, will not do. In our view there must be on the part of the federal government a major commitment to move in the housing sector with significant sums of money to increase supply so that the cost of housing can be brought down.
Those are the principal reasons why our party opposes this specific set of proposals. Some of my colleagues will be giving additional points. I have tried to indicate the principal ones. To sum up, in our judgment there is unfairness on the one hand and there is unworkability on the other hand. We say that the package which has been brought in to deal with inflation is deficient in terms both of what it prescribes and what it lacks, particularly in relation to housing, pensioners, and low income Canadians.
I wish to turn now to the reasons why the government feels it must bring this kind of program before the people of Canada at this time. The white paper, the former Minister of Finance, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson), and the Prime Minister himself have referred to two issues. One is the wage-push factor in inflation and the other is the problem as they perceive it of our pricing ourselves out of competitive markets. The New Democratic Party takes both these points seriously. If they could be demonstrated, then the government's intention to base remedies on these particular ills would be entirely appropriate. What I want to argue is that in fact they do not have the foundation that the government claims they have, that we do not have inflation in Canada which is due to high wage demands, and that we do not have in Canada a serious threat to our competitive position in terms of world trade because of such wage demands and wage increases.
October 14, 1975

In my view there is no economist, respectable or otherwise, in Canada who has demonstrated a cause and effect relationship between our wages and our inflation. Many workers in Canada, trapped by two and three year contracts, have been merely attempting to make up the ground they lost due to past inflation. In the last three years, from mid June 1972 to mid June 1975, the consumer price index rose by 33 per cent. During the same period of time wages rose by 36 per cent, or only 1 per cent more a year. Given increases in Canadian labour productivity I would argue that the Canadian worker has in fact got less than he deserves, not more. Certainly I would argue that he has not caused the inflation that was going on in the Canadian economy; he was responding to it.

I am pleased to add to my support a person whom I and the socialist party would not normally be citing, that is, Gerald Bouey, Governor of the Bank of Canada, who made a speech about a week ago in Saskatoon in which he made essentially the same point. I think it is very important to get through to the people in our country who now are beginning to see ordinary working Canadians as being the principal cause of our economic problems that that is not the case. The Governor of the Bank of Canada himself said that wage demands in recent years have followed price increases, that workers have not been causing the increases, that they have been responding to them; in short, they have been responding to the mismanagement of the Canadian economy.
What about the trade situation? Again we have heard a number of politicians, editorial writers and businessmen complain about Canadian wage settlements. What are the facts? First of all, a recent study by Nathan Bossen of the Montreal brokerage firm of Brault, Guy, O'Brien, Inc.-not a well known socialist establishment-using figures from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, concluded that Canadian unit labour costs from 1970 to the beginning of 1975 have escalated at a lower rate than those of any of our major trading partners with the exception of the United States. In Bossen's view:
Canadian unit costs have not risen at such a rate as to cause concern for our competitive position.
In any event, relative labour cost increases seem to have little bearing on trade performance; real demand for a country's export products is more important. This is particularly true when the principal exports are raw materials, as is the case with Canada. It does not matter in any significant degree what the labour costs are in terms of our major exports. But I repeat the point: even if, as is the case in certain sectors, labour costs are a concern, our competitive situation has been improving, not getting worse, and I will provide some more information on that.
The 7 per cent decline in exports over the past year is due to an international recession and not to the loss of our ability to compete. The United States is our largest customer, and when the United States is suffering a recession Canadian exports will also decline because demand in the United States has dropped. Furthermore, recent import-export statistics refute those who have been saying that
Anti-Inflation
high wage settlements in Canada are pricing our exports out of other markets than the United States. Exports of Canadian finished products with a relatively high labour component have increased in value by 8 per cent in the first six months of this year; all exports, including raw materials, rose only 5 per cent. So the increase in our exports has been going up higher in those sectors than in all exports as a whole.
If trade in automotive goods to the United States is excluded from the figures, the performance of the manufactured goods sector looks even better, with exports up during this period by some 13 per cent. Trade indices also show that between January, 1974, and the end of March, 1975, prices of Canadian exports rose by an average of 27 per cent while import prices increased by 42 per cent. This means that our relative competitive position in terms of prices in world trade has improved, not worsened.
I defy the new Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, when he contributes to this debate, as I hope he will, to present some supporting evidence for the case that his predecessor has made, namely, that we are pricing ourselves out of world markets.
I notice, Madam Speaker, that you are rising to your feet, so perhaps I will call it six o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, if this were the day before Christmas we would say: In the silence of the night, let us all reflect on the future of our country. But since this is October 14, 1975, let us all reflect on the economy of our country.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to use seriously the few minutes allotted to me to express the views and the wishes of the voters of the constituency of Bellechasse that I proudly represent, and also to express the thought of, I believe, all Canadians who are concerned about the future of Canada so that the economy of our country may serve all Canadian citizens and that we may serve our country as Canadians.
When, a few years ago, President Kennedy fell under the bullets of an assassin, these words of his were recalled on several occasions: We must not ask what this country can do for us, Americans, but rather what we, as American citizens, can do for our country. Mr. Speaker, these words should apply in 1975. We should ask ourselves very seriously: What have we done for our country? What has Canada done for each one of us? What does the future hold for us

October 14, 1975
Anti-Inflation
as a nation? What does Canada hold for each one of us in the future? What must each one of us do to ensure the future, the greatness and the development of our country? October 14, 1975 is a memorable day in the history of our country.
We can have fun and amuse ourselves, go to the movies or to the theatre, we can act irresponsibly if we wish, but it still remains, Mr. Speaker, that a serious decision must be made in our country on this day, October 14. We must make this decision together, you, Mr. Speaker, each one of my colleagues of the House of Commons, and this parliament, we must seriously ask ourselves what the population is thinking tonight at 8:10 about the Canadian parliament, and it is wondering how we shall determine the future of every Canadian and of our economy.
Mr. Speaker, as I keep constantly in touch with my constituents, my fellow countrymen, I can tell you that these people are now worried. The fathers, mothers and heads of families are concerned about the future of their children. They are wondering what is in store for tomorrow.
What do the children we have brought into the world, we have raised and given the best training we could, the best education possible at every level, think of us today and what will happen to them tomorrow?
Mr. Speaker, some authorities are also wondering, the municipal authorities which are closer to the people, which assume the greatest responsibilities towards the individuals and families are now wondering how they will manage to provide the services to which the families and the individuals are entitled.
Recently a convention of the Canadian Federation of Municipalities was held. Through its most authoritative spokesmen, its president and its executive secretary in turn expressed their concern to the people, the federal and provincial authorities, having to meet their obligations and provide essential services to the people.
Recently, we have also witnessed a congress of mayors of municipalities. I feel quite at ease in speaking of municipal affairs because I have been directly involved in them for over 30 years. I think I know pretty well the thinking of mayors, secretary-treasurers, aldermen of cities and towns, and rural municipality counsellors. I believe I can feel the pulse of the situation.
All these people during these congresses, and in particular, the congress of mayors and municipalities, were concerned by a terrible situation.
People across the country are asking municipal authorities essential services, such as sewers, aqueducts, housing, but such services at prices and conditions they can afford.
About a week ago, I saw the mayor of the city of Quebec say to the people on television that if the provinces cannot adequately meet the requirements and demands of municipalities the latter would have to turn to Ottawa, and Ottawa, Mr. Speaker, it is you, Ottawa, it is all the members of Parliament, it is the right hon. Prime Minister, all the ministers of the various Canadian government departments.
While we have heard many times during the last 20 years that the autonomy of municipalities is something sacred like that of provinces, since the provincial governments are unable to meet their financial requirements adequately, the municipalities are now pondering their problems. I take to witness the mayor of Quebec City who a week ago stated: If the provinces are unable to help us, we shall have to turn to Ottawa. Ottawa, it is you Mr. Speaker and all of us now in session to examine very seriously the problems facing us.
The municipal government is the one that is closest to the people, that can best understand the needs of individuals and families and normally it should be in a position to answer adequately the legitimate requirements of individuals and families. But we know that municipalities are now in a desperate financial situation. Reading the newspapers is enough to convince us that those situations are desperate in Canada. If we take a look at the United States, we realize that New York City, Boston and other big American cities are at the brink of bankruptcy. What does it mean, Mr. Speaker, to be on the verge of bankruptcy? It is to have expenses in excess of the potential income a given community would need to meet its normal financial obligations. In the meantime, we as Canadians, as Quebecers, as the Quebec government, we crawl in front of New York financiers begging for help. When they are not even able to meet their obligations, we ask them to lend us money to survive at home, to survive as a province, to survive as a country, to survive as municipalities.
Mr. Speaker, this clearly demonstrates that the problem we confront today as Canadian parliamentarians boils down to two things: inflation and unemployment, which are both financial problems. These days a lot is being said about inflation. But great care is taken not to define inflation. Reporters, newspapers, television and radio do not co-operate very much with you, Mr. Speaker, and with hon. members to enlighten the Canadian public as to what inflation really is. As for me I am not smart but I know that I am not smart. There is something which is great, it is to be aware of it. And I can always go to the people who are more learned than I am. Larousse is a dictionary which defines all the words in the French language and which tells you what each and every one of them means. That is why, not being smart tonight I opened my Larousse dictionary. And I have tried to find out what inflation means. So here is what one can read in the Larousse dictionary, on page 543. Let us listen well, Mr. Speaker. I may not be very bright but surely Larousse knows what it is all about. I quote:
Inflation: Desequilibre economique earacterise par une hausse generale des prix, et qui provient de l'exces de pouvoir d'achat de la masse des consommateurs (particuliers, entreprises ...) . .. et des services mis a leur disposition.
So, this means that there is an increase, an excess of purchasing power in relation to services offered to people and goods available to them. That is what inflation means.
