services offered to people, is there an excess of potatoes, tomatoes, pork, milk, butter, cheese?
If I had the time to do so, Mr. Speaker, I would pick out of our own Hansard answers which prove that in the last few months we did import cheese from New Zealand, Australia, the United States, Holland and Belgium, and that we also imported beef from those various countries. Therefore, was there really a surplus of those farm produce, considering the demands of the consumer, the needs of the Canadian consumers? That is what the Larousse dictionary says: excessive purchasing power, too much money to buy the goods that are lacking.
And at the same time, Mr. Speaker, the producers of Canadian cheese and butter are told: Reduce your production; quotas will be imposed upon you; you will be forced to produce according to a specific quota system, to avoid surplus production exceeding the purchasing power of Canadians.
Do you know, Mr. Speaker, what is happening at the same time? While poultry producers are told to reduce their production, are asked to accept quotas, the same organizations tell the Americans to come and sell in Quebec, in Canada, their surplus poultry, their surplus eggs, that we will accept them here; that is what causes the imbalance, that is what explains the fact that our producers of beef, pork, poultry and eggs, do not know where they stand, and which way to go; their situation is hopeless; they can no longer get for their work, their production, the income needed to live decently. This is happening in Canada, before the eyes of all parliamentarians, myself included, and we look on passively. Then the Prime Minister, on the eve of two by-elections, appears on television, as the leader of the Canadian government and of a political party called the Liberal party, and sets forth to the Canadian people solutions to our problems of inflation and unemployment. He tells them: Boys, there is only one answer, tighten your belts. I have a belt too and if I tighten it, I will choke eventually. Now, tighten your belts.
What does he mean by tightening our belts? It is to go without the things one needs to meet one's personal needs. That is to tighten one's belt. Is the solution proposed in the white paper a good solution? The Canadian Parliament must decide on this this week. Is it really the answer to the economic problems, to the problems of inflation and unemployment in our country? Is it the answer? What is unemployment? Since I am not smart, I consult those who are more learned. What does unemployment mean? On page 206, Larousse says: Period of inactivity for a worker, for an industry. We knew that also. To be unemployed means being out of work, that is what we must remember, Mr. Speaker. To be unemployed means being out of work. I would like to look fully into that question. I heard last night on television the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) say to the Canadian people that our gross national product must increase if we are to deal with the problems of inflation and unemployment. I may not be very knowledgeable about those things, but I am at my wits' end to understand what he meant by that.
Mr. Speaker, quite seriously, I will speak about the
budget of the former Minister of Finance, the hon. member
Anti-Inflation
for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner), which was brought down on June 23, 1975. I was sitting in my place, he was in his, and the others were in theirs. We were waiting, holding our breath, for the solutions to our economic problems. Nobody, Mr. Speaker, is happy with adverse conditions in Canada, nobody is happy about that, regardless of one's party. We want Canada to have a really prosperous economy which would enable fathers, mothers, boys and girls who have been educated at the cost of hundreds of dollars-I know it from experience-after obtaining their diploma and acquiring experience in their chosen field to serve the Canadian community and the country, thanks to that diploma and that profession which make them efficient producers of either services or goods in a given line.
I think it is only good common sense that leads us to expect from our children, from the coming generation to produce things to meet the needs of the population as a whole. We know what is going on, Mr. Speaker. We have now more than 600,000 qualified people, graduates who hold diplomas or trade certificates and could be productive, but they are unfortunately out of work. It was said earlier what unemployment is. It is to be unproductive. People are prevented from using their talents to produce something in order to meet their needs or those of the community.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in the budget of 1975-76, I think some thought should be given to that. I apologize for speaking up but I am shocked, you understand, Mr. Speaker, I am shocked to see that we are going to spend- responsible people like the Postmaster General (Mr. Mack-asey), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and all cabinet members, responsible people-that we are to spend in 1975-76 nearly $4 billion to support unproductive people, to pay benefits to people who willy-nilly are unemployed, idle. Meanwhile, Mr. Speaker, they try to make the public believe the unemployment problem can be solved, that jobs can be created and that the $150 million earmarked for local initiative programs will generate employment throughout Canada.
A sixth grade school boy, Mr. Speaker, can do better than spending $150 million to motivate people to work, to do something to increase the gross national product in this country, to meet our obligations, to curb the curse of inflation so as to provide Canadians with an ever increasing number of goods and services and lick this serious problem of inflation.
Mr. Speaker, I have read very carefully, and when I say very carefully I mean very earnestly because at my age one is not interested in jesting any more. When one has family commitments such as I have at present, such as I have had in the past, a lot of things become less important if considered intrinsically. They belong to the past. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I believe we should very seriously consider the solutions which are proposed in the white paper. "White paper" is a beautiful expression. What is white is supposed to be pure, but in the final analysis, as once said the former President of France, the late General de Gaulle whose name I proudly utter, regardless of the mistakes he

October 14. 1975
Anti-Inflation
may have made-at least words I did not mean should not be put in my mouth-at least he gave mankind the very profound thought that one should always get to the bottom of things. Whatever the matter, Mr. Speaker, our responsibility is to get to the root of it to find out about the formula that is proposed to us, the valid solution to our problems. Is the white paper presented to us today the right formula to solve inflation and unemployment? I ask the question, dear fellow members of Parliament. Let us try to think about it seriously. I know that as a member of a small political party, opponents take pleasure in telling us we are a small political party. Mr. Speaker, in a family of any size, when the little one tells the authorities: It is raining this morning, even if the authorities say that the sun is shining, if it is really raining, the little one is right. That is the way it is in Parliament.
In Parliament, Mr. Speaker, we sincerely declare that the formulas proposed by the economists until now are not valid. The right hon. Prime Minister of my country that I respect whole heartedly has been misinformed by the economists. The Cabinet of my country whatever the colour of the governing party has been misinformed by the economists of our country: they say first one thing and then another. Some say: Let us try this formula and if it does not work, we shall try another one. In the meantime, Canadians are the ones who pay.
Mr. Speaker, we are in a really desperate economic situation. Canada has got into debt and I bring your attention to this: From 1867 to 1967, our debt has gradually reached $30 billion. It has taken a hundred years to accumulate a debt of $30 billion. You can check, Mr. Speaker. It was the official answer of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) as reported in Hansard this year. The debt of our country that amounted to $30 billion as of July 1, 1967 has reached $58 billion as of July 1, 1974. By now I would not be surprised if our national debt has reached $60 billion.
Mr. Speaker, this is the essence of my remarks for tonight. I took a roundabout way to demonstrate to my colleagues that the main cause of inflation is the financial system in which we live, that no longer meets our needs in 1975 and contributes to raise the cost of living because of interest rates which go up every month.
Mr. Speaker, as I speak to you and every morning the sun rises Canadians in this country must make sacrifices, pay $10 million in interests on the national debt, and I challenge any member in this House to prove otherwise because those are official figures released by Statistics Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the way things are going, we are moving toward an even more catastrophic situation. So what does a small party like the Social Credit Party of Canada suggest? Mr. Speaker, you seem to say, just a few members. I can tell you that in this little party we are serious, we love our country as much as any other member of this House. We want our country to be prosperous and we also want every member of this country, whatever the wealth of the family to which they belong, we want every Canadian to be able to share the benefits of the sacrifices and
efforts of past generations. We are disgusted, Mr. Speaker, when we see that this parliament, this government, has helped bring about such a disastrous situation.
Mr. Speaker, a week ago the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) ask the people of Canada, to tighten their belt, to be reasonable in your claims. I fully agree with him but he forgot, for example, that the day before, Canadian bankers enjoyed an increase of 1 per cent in the interest rate. Did you think of what that represents for the whole of Canada, an increase of 1 per cent on all loans made not only in the public sector but also the private sector?
Mr. Speaker, in the present situation in which we live the federal and provincial governments are private industry's main competitors. My dear friends, it is an excellent formula which enables a country to develop, because private enterprise allows the individual and the enterprise to give the best of themselves, to use their abilities and their resources to the fullest and thus not only the individual, but his family as well as his community may derive some benefit.
Mr. Speaker, I am quite sincere when I say that we have a golden opportunity to change our economic system.
Our Prime Minister, whom I respect and to whom I listened on television last night, did not give us any magic formula, but he called upon the goodwill of the individuals as I do tonight to use another formula. The Prime Minister did not suggest any new approach. What is preventing us from trying something new since we are at our lowest ebb and quite unable up to now to try such an experiment. What is that new experiment? It consists in the use by the Canadian government, backed by Parliament which is the supreme authority in our country, in the use, as I said, of the Bank of Canada. Some people think it is funny. You see those green Liberal members making faces and becoming exhilarated whenever Social Credit members suggest a better way of making use of that bank which belongs to the Canadian people as a means of creating credit, as a means of turning the dedication of each and everyone of us into money, as a means of having that dedication turned out into dollars and benefit Canadian citizens as a whole. We therefore introduced an amendment to the Bank of Canada Act so that this Bank which was created by Liberals-Why not at least try to trust your own party.

My God, how pleased I am, Mr. Speaker, to hear the Chair ask my colleagues in the House to let the member for Bellechasse complete his speech. I will not abuse this privilege, believe me! My feelings are well known. It is therefore common experience that during the eight or ten years I have sat as a member of this House, I have never attempted to abuse the privileges of the House. Mr. Speaker, I thank you and I thank my colleagues for letting me complete my remarks.

October 14, 1975

I was just saying that the Government should be allowed for once to use the Bank of Canada as a means of managing the credit of our nation, of providing new credit, of paying the discount that we suggest as a solution to our present economic problems. A compensated discount is the opposite of a tax. A 10 per cent tax has the effect of increasing prices by 10 per cent, whereas a compensated discount cuts down prices by 10 per cent. The 10 per cent discount benefits all those who use those products. But who is going to pay for that discount? The whole of the Canadian people through the Bank of Canada, the national credit board, will determine that Canadians have worked more, that the country's output has increased. In 1974 our gross national product amounted to $139 billion. But if in 1975 our national product is $140 billion, the increase should benefit all Canadians. And in order that every Canadian may benefit, it should be distributed as dividends, as guaranteed annual income or as another form of revenue.
This, Mr. Speaker, may seem funny to you, but we sincerely believe in such a measure. We are convinced such a formula would be no worse than all the damn formulas tried to date, and which have led to the present failure. Let us have the courage to try something new. We cannot do any worse than what we have known until now.

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spoke to the nation yesterday evening on television, he asked Canadians to act in a responsible and collective way to deal with the serious economic problems now facing Canada.
The white paper tabled today proposes a series of strong and courageous measures to stop inflation. It is clear that our economy is now besieged by too much inflation. But it is just as clear that there is too much unemployment, and that we should have continued growth while maintaining a social reform program. I say without any hesitation that the government needed a great deal of courage to resist the pressures by those who would have wanted us to use a big stick against inflation, by imposing a freeze on price and wages, whatever the cost to the growth and welfare of our economy, and by making such drastic cuts in government expenditures that the most basic social and economic policies would have suffered.
Instead, the government has opted for a four point program: first, the fiscal and monetary policy will be administered so as to increase global demand and production at a rate consistent with that of an increasingly regressing inflation and there is absolutely no question of using unemployment as an antidote to inflationary forces.
Second, the growth of federal government expenses will be restricted to what we believe the economy of the country can support. It is obvious that the manpower of the public service will not be able to increase substantially and will therefore increase little, but it is also obvious that the government will maintain essential services and allowances, particularly for those who need them most.
Third, the government recognizes that the present inflationary forces are profoundly entrenched in the structure of the goods and services and labour markets, as well as in
Anti-inflation
the attitudes and the expectations of the population. Our labour and goods and services markets are not as effective as they should be. We must therefore make our economy more dynamic and more effective by reducing the present rigidity and intensifying competition in Canada.
These are important concerns which enormously affect my department. If we want to eradicate in the long run the latent danger of inflation, we shall have to develop a whole series of special measures in the areas of food, energy, and housing which will affect the very structures of these areas.
Fourth, the program of the government aims at taking decisive action to overcome the present inflationary psychology by following for the first time since the Second World War a clear and precise policy concerning prices and incomes in Canada.
This policy was used as a guideline to restrict the margins of profits, prices, dividends and salaries in Canada. It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that we recognize the inconsistency of the present inflation rate with the public interest as well as the seriousness of the national problem involved in its control and reversal.
That is why the Prime Minister asked the provincial premiers for their support and urged all Canadians to stand by those guidelines. That is why the Prime Minister also indicated that he hopes that those who hold the economic power in our society will respect those guidelines. That those who hold the economic power, that is his government, the governments of all provinces, the business and labour sectors will strictly comply with that guideline. That is why an anti-inflation board has been set up. It will have to see that this policy is respected. And finally, that is why later this week my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) will introduce legislation to establish the mechanism and provide the necessary powers to force some groups in our society to abide by the guideline, if they do not move volontarily.
Mr. Speaker, I think that in proposing those new economic measures, the government has adopted a responsible and firm position which will allow the Canadian people to go through, without too much trouble, that transitional period and, let us admit it, that period of economic difficulties. It aims at changing the inflation trends without throwing the economy into serious recession. It calls for some restraint from those who seek higher prices and incomes, particularly the big companies, the labour and public sectors, instead of using coercion and a large bureaucracy to reach those objectives. We believe indeed that Canadians would like to shoulder their own responsibility in cooperating with us instead of letting the government get unduly involved in individual and corporate affairs.
I listened very carefully this afternoon to the remarks of
the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) who
said that controls had to be comprehensive. For many

minutes during his speech he tried to tell us that this is exactly what we now have, and he tried to tell us that what he proposed to the Canadian people sometime ago is what the government has now offered the Canadian public.

He said it was important to change the thinking of Canadians who feel that in order to get their piece of cake they must protect themselves against inflation by asking for more. Therefore, when we issue these guidelines we issue them on a voluntary basis applicable to everyone, but we say that the big ones, those who have a significant effect on the economy, must obey a certain set of selective rules, and if they do not there is legislation to be used to put things in order.
I was completely surprised and shocked by the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition when he said the Prime Minister should not try to teach us but should show us. He went on moralizing and so on, and attempted to imply that we are not giving leadership.
[Mr. Ouellet.J
I want to place on record first that the Prime Minister and the other ministers will obey the guidelines. This is clear. I do not appreciate what was said last night on the national network that there will be two sets of guidelines, one for the Canadian people and another for the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister and the ministers will obey the guidelines.
Second, I believe it is important not only to talk but to show leadership. The Prime Minister said that these guidelines will apply to federal public servants, a clear-cut indication that he hopes the provincial governments will have the courage to do the same.
Third, the growth of the public service will be limited. This has been said, and it is important that this be done.
Fourth, the total spending by the Canadian government will not rise out of proportion to the trend in respect of the gross national product. The Leader of the Official Opposition this afternoon read from page 8 of the document "Attack on inflation". This quotation is as follows:
The federal government shares the view that the trend of total spending by all governments in Canada should not rise more quickly than the trend of the gross national product.
He said he does not understand what that means. Surely he should have read the two previous pages and looked particularly at the government's expenditures as a percentage of the gross national product. In fact he should have realized that the total expenditures of all governments in Canada as a percentage of the gross national product have increased to a great degree throughout the years 1965 to 1974. This is the sort of trend about which many people in the business community in Canada have complained. Many people and many members of the opposition have complained about the fact that the federal government and other governments are spending too much. This is the sort of thing with which we are trying to cope.
Surely, however, when we talk of our spending and the sort of things we could do to reduce our spending, the Leader of the Opposition is not suggesting that we should completely phase out some of our commitments that are of a statutory nature. I want to remind hon. members in this House that in fact some 56 per cent of the budgetary expenditures approved for the start of the fiscal year 1975-76 are for statutory programs. Another 9 per cent is accounted for by such essential support programs as consumer subsidies on petroleum products, programs relating to Indians and Eskimos, grants for regional economic expansion, incentives to increase manufacturing, and subsidies to farmers.
There is no doubt that the government will do its utmost to limit expenditures, but not at the expense of the poor people of Canada, those living in remote areas of Canada, and those who are in the greatest need in this society.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to greet you as you are taking up your duties for the first time. I am sure that on behalf of all the members, I may extend to you our best wishes in the performance of your new duties.
October 14, 1975

Mr. Speaker, I am rising this evening mainly to state to the House the crucial role that the Anti-Inflation Board will have to play to create a climate of restraint and moderation and to ensure that those who will readily restrain their price and income increases are not victimized because some powerful sectors of our economy will choose to ignore the rule of the game. I think that it is quite proper to put this Board under the responsibility of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, because under its terms of reference, it must protect the competitive power of the economy while ensuring its efficiency and see to it that the profits derived from production are fairly distributed among the producer, distributor and consumer.
Mr. Speaker, the terms of reference and duties of the Board will be as follows:
First, to monitor movements in prices, profits, compensation and dividends. It will be responsible for examining them in the light of the policy set forth by the government. It will report to the government on the efficiency and the workability of this policy, and make such recommendations for its modification that it deems necessary.
Second, to. identify actual or proposed movements in prices, profits, compensation and dividends which it feels violate the policy proposed by the government.
It will determine to what extent such movements can have a significant impact on the economy and if so, it will bring together the parties involved and endeavour through negotiations and consultations to bring them within the limits and the spirit of the government policy.
Thirdly, should the parties involved refuse to comply voluntarily with the government policy requirements and if they are liable to the legal restraints provided under this policy, the matter will be referred to the administrator of the anti-inflation act. The latter will investigate the matter and if he finds that the government policy was contravened without good reason, he will order a rollback to the initial price and the refund of all amounts paid beyond the limits set under the said policy.
Fourthly and lastly, the Anti-Inflation Board will feel duty bound to promote greater understanding of the inflationary process by arranging public hearings and meetings, by publishing reports, and by other means that it considers helpful. All such reports will be tabled in the House of Commons and made available to the public.
According to its terms of reference, Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the government is not trying to use this Board as an instrument of dictatorship in the economic area. Its main purpose is more like that of a watchdog or a peacemaker. The voluntary acceptance of the government policy will be emphasized, so that the need for a more specific legislation and a closer monitoring will not be felt. We shall give those the Board will deem necessary to investigate every opportunity to justify their behaviour and to mend their ways according to the limits of the government policy.
One of the main duties of the Board will be to define and interpret the government policy in order to apply it to every individual case. It will interpret and define the
Anti-inflation
public interest under such circumstances, whether it be a major increase in prices or salaries during collective bargaining. It will monitor the actions of those who regulate the pace of our economy, big business and collective bargaining both in the public and the private sectors. It will make every effort to bring those who are about to disregard the government policy to adhere to the standard guidelines. However, should persuasion fail and if the parties involved refuse to comply with the policy set forth by the government, the Board will have the necessary authority to recommend the enforcement of the law.
I would like at this point to reply to some remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) when he said that so far as he is concerned the price control methods that have been outlined by the government are no good and will not operate. He expressed great doubt and great skepticism about what we have put in place. I want to tell him that I have more faith in the plan. I believe that the price controls will be effective, and I want to tell him, as well as other hon. members in the House, that before passing such quaint judgment on the scheme they should at least wait until they see the legislation and then the regulations. I think that then they would be in a better position to pass judgment and condemn or praise the plan.
I have more faith than the hon. member in the anti-inflation review board, and I have much greater faith than he expressed this afternoon in the members of that board. I also have more faith in the person named to be the administrator of the scheme, the official who will have the authority to act and who will have all the tools necessary to ensure that the price control mechanisms which we might want to use if necessary can be used effectively.

My colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has already stated that later this week he would bring forward a legislation which would give to the governor general in council the power to formulate a policy relating to restrictions with respect to higher profit margins, dividends and salaries, to set up an anti-inflation board, as I have already indicated, and to give to its president the powers which will allow him to apply the government's policy to specific groups.
Moreover, it has been decided that the setting up of this board should not be delayed. So, an order in council has been passed this very morning which established on a temporary basis the composition of the anti-inflation board. This temporary board will be maintained until a permanent anti-inflation board is established, that is until the legislation is passed by Parliament. This interim Board will then become the Anti-Inflation Board.
I am pleased, Mr. Speaker, to confirm that two well-known and highly respectable and respected Canadian citizens have accepted, at the invitation of the Prime Minister, to sit on that Board. The chairman of the Board the hon. Jean-Luc Pepin is not a stranger to the House. Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
October 14, 1975
Anti-inflation
Pepin will bring to the Board an invaluable knowledge of the machinery of government and business management, as well as a good dose of patience and a lot of good humour. The vice-chairman will be the present chairman of the Food Prices Review Board, Mrs. Beryl Plumptre. She has accepted to serve for an interim period long enough to terminate on the one hand the unfinished reports of the Food Prices Review Board and on the other hand to help set up and give a solid start to the new Board. Thanks to her exceptional leadership qualities the Food Prices Review Board has largely contributed I think to educate the people making them aware of the causes of inflation in the food area. I am convinced that she will keep on speaking her mind frankly, quality that personally I greatly appreciate. Furthermore, we have already started to recruit a competent staff in order to allow the Board to immediately get to work. In addition, the government intends to enlarge the membership of the Board so as to include representatives of various regions. This de-centralization will ease the task of the Board which will be able, because of the personal experience of its members, to take into account in its proceedings, situations prevailing in various areas of the country.
Hon. members have probably noticed, while looking at the White Paper, that the federal government has already started to comply with its own recommendations as far as the Crown corporations and federal agencies are concerned. The Prime Minister asked the provincial governments to take this action. The Anti-inflation board will be responsible for imposing the same requirements upon the public sector as upon the private sector.
To this end, the board will create for the public sector a distinct office that will handle price and wage matters. The provinces have been invited to appoint members to that office. The order in council creating the temporary antiinflation board put an end to the work of the Food Prices Review Board. In just over two years, this agency has published more than 40 reports and it will be possible to publish the reports that have reached the final writing, translation or even the printing stage. I wish to say tonight that this agency, through its participation in the public debate on the food prices policy, has given the population a better understanding of such a difficult problem. I wish to thank publicly the members of that board for their excellent work. The experience of the Plumptre Board will not be lost as a good part of its staff will be integrated into the new anti-inflation board.
Mr. Speaker, before I conclude my speech, I wish to recall that the measures we are taking today are those of a government determined to act in a constructive way to improve the economic situation. However, I would be remiss if in my capacity as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs I did not draw the attention of this House on two legislative steps undertaken by my department and which will have a long term impact as far as curbing inflation is concerned. I refer first to the reform of the competition policy in Canada and second, to consumer credit.
I think the reform of the Combines Investigation Act was the most important element of the steps taken by this government to conform with the structure of the economy,

particularly when one knows that the contrary itself is responsible for a good part for the inflation we have.
The white paper also emphasizes the fact that this country needs greater market competition. The current legislation is outmoded and several of its provisions are no longer in line with the current modern world. I am happy to know that under an agreement with opposition members we can look forward to the rapid passage of Bill C-2 this week in the House of Commons, and I hope members of the other House will understand that it is important to approve this bill quickly and will cooperate with the government in that respect. Preparation of Phase II of the competition policy is practically completed, and we are getting ready to publish it later on this year. The proposals will reflect the judgment of the most enlightened Canadians on competition, and should clarify the question. After a reasonable period of discussion and debate, it is my intention to table a bill during the next session.
I also believe another major piece of legislation could help Canadians face the price increases. I am referring to the precise evaluation of their credit needs. Too often, unfortunately, consumers do not know the real cost of credit and tend to underestimate its impact on the family budget. It is so easy to use a credit card and forget that there are less costly ways of financing one's purchases. In my belief, it is the government's duty to ensure there is adequate disclosure of credit costs, such disclosure as not to require the use of a computer to compare various financing means.
The consumers must be informed of the best method available to them to lower their credit costs. Therefore, I intend to propose to the House a legislation concerning the protection of borrowers. That new legislation will provide for adequate protection for small borrowers. Also, my department is setting up programs aimed at helping consumers, particularly those who have low incomes, in order that they use credit in a more appropriate way. The legislation will also offer better protection for those who are involved with usurious moneylenders. I am convinced that careful and sensible use of credit will help many Canadians come through this difficult period.
Mr. Speaker, the new economic measures taken by the government are based on the belief that Canadians will give a constructive answer to the invitation of the Prime Minister and that they will accept to get together to slow down the price and income increases and also the excessive pressures which have jeopardized the economy. As I said, the anti-inflation board will play an important part in that government price and income policy.
This will not bring about undue government interference in the economy.
Those who accept voluntarily to submit to government policy will be assured that they will not become the victims of unscrupulous manipulators.
Finally, this will provide sufficient flexibility to adjust to economic fluctuations while our economy is on the uprise.
Mr. Speaker, I believe this anti-inflation policy to be a wise policy which meets the present needs of the Canadi-
October 14, 1975

an economy and provides what a great majority of Canadians wished for from the central government, and I am convinced that despite the disfigurement by the opposition of this general program, of this government attack program on inflation, despite the very understandable disfigurement by the Progressive Conservative Party, which would like people to believe that we are imposing a comprehensive and complete control on prices and incomes, the great majority of Canadians will understand that these are selective measures, but also guidelines, which must apply voluntarily in Canada and which, I am sure, will be followed by the great majority of Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stevens:
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
As I listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last night on television, I wanted to believe what he was saying. I earnestly hoped that the government was on the verge of launching an anti-inflationary program in this nation. But having read the remarks of the Prime Minister, the highlights of the anti-inflation program of th^ government, and the anti-inflation program itself, I
Anti-inflation
find it difficult to match the words of the government with its previous actions. We have heard this rhetoric before. We have heard the Prime Minister lamenting that somehow it is others in the private sector who are causing the problem, but not the government.
For example, on November 2, 1969-that is a long time ago-the Prime Minister went on the television program "The Nation's Business" and stated:
... the situation is an inflationary one. And that is why such a large thrust of all the government's policies is concerned with breaking the back of inflation. We as a government have taken various steps, balancing our budget-even having a surplus.
I wonder how he accounts for the $5 billion deficit this year alone when he talks about surpluses? Most interesting of all, on November 2, 1969, he went on to state:
We have had a monetary policy, a fiscal policy, which shows that we are doing our part.
He pointed his finger at various sectors of the economy and stated that it is the duty of the government to talk for all these little people ... It is the business of the government to speak for them. "We are doing it by telling big companies and big unions if they do not follow the government's example-and its voluntary restraint-we will take some action."
He went on to say:
We can spend more money. But we want to have our operations responsible. We don't want to increase taxes, therefore we don't want to have a deficit.
Finally he stated:
It is private enterprise, it is the private sector of the economy and in this I include the big unions, who are not doing their share.
How similar that is to the words of last night. He went on to state:
Because they have strong bargaining power they're trying to get a big slice of the cake and pass on the results of their greed to the little people. What we're saying now is that if they don't take their responsibilities, the government will take its.
Before we go further in this debate let us recall what has been the record of the government with respect to the items referred to in this speech by the Prime Minister. He refers to deficits, government spending, fiscal policy, and monetary policy. Here is the record.
Since the Prime Minister took power in April, 1968, the money supply in this country has risen by an astounding 111 per cent, a 15 per cent increase in the last 12 months alone. In the same period we find that inflation has gone up 58 per cent. This is the inflation that the Prime Minister spoke of breaking back in 1969.
Perhaps most significantly during this period, the government's own spending has jumped by 192 per cent, it has almost doubled, yet in 1969 we had a prime minister who had the nerve to suggest that his government in future years was going to be a government of restraint with respect to monetary growth and government spending. That is why, although I would earnestly hope that the government would accept its responsibility and tackle inflation in this country in an effective way, I believe we have grounds for doubt that its members are serious in their present stance with respect to inflation.

October 14, 1975
Anti-inflation
In my view, Mr. Speaker, there are several parts to a proper, comprehensive anti-inflationary program. The monetary stance of the government is one thing, its fiscal stance on government spending is a second. The trade policy of the government has got to change-that too is part of a proper inflation policy. There is no industrial strategy in this country, yet last night we heard no suggestion that the new Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) was going to come up with any new direction for our industry.
In this debate, especially when the bill is before us, I think we should press the government to explain more fully to what extent it is going to cut out some of the government regulations that frustrate business in this country at the present time.
I believe some consideration should also be given to, and action taken on, where we can relieve some of the overlapping jurisdictional problems that exist in the country at the federal, provincial and municipal levels. This is one of the bottlenecks and we are not being told in detail of any government plans to relieve this problem.
Finally, I would suggest that in any anti-inflationary program the government should be willing to outline the position it intends to take in international circles among the large industrial nations to ensure that there is a concerted effort among those nations to counter inflation in the western world.
I should like to go back to those eight points in due course, but before we consider the program that was outlined last night and more fully described in the white paper today, we should check once again the wording of the budget speech delivered by the former minister of finance on June 23 this year. As we know, throughout the presentation today and yesterday the government made frequent references to this June 23 budget, and you will recall that in making their presentation both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) quoted quite extensively from that speech. What they did not say was that the then minister of finance dealt with the concept of controls on June 23. Here is what the then minister of finance said:
We gave careful consideration to the imposition of statutory controls over prices and incomes.
He went on to explain that he felt that there was some possibility that those controls would, in principle, be acceptable at that time. He continued:
But there would have been-and are-immense difficulties and disadvantages in such a course of action.
That is referring specifically to the type of control we now have before us. The minister of finance of that date stated:
Government would have to interfere in every type of business decision and wage settlement. To a far greater extent than in a voluntary program, a new bureaucratic apparatus would have to be set up. New types of inequity would be created. The flexibility of the market economy in directing resources where they are most needed would be impaired. Dislocations would occur.
The minister went on to state:
These costs would be worth paying if direct controls could be successfully imposed. If this were the case, we might well achieve lower price and cost increases without higher unemployment. But the success of
such a program would depend crucially on widespread public support. As I have said before, I believe that we can resort to direct controls only when there is a public conviction of the need for such action. That point has not been reached.
That was the government's view on June 23. What has changed? What has changed now other than the minister of finance? Is there this public support that the former minister of finance felt that they needed before bringing in the controls that we now have? Judging from the comments of labour leaders last night, it would appear not. I simply state that we seem to have a very inconsistent pattern in the government's policy concerning the program that it is now asking us to accept.
I understand that the powers to be are to be given discretion, as an integral part of the anti-inflation program, to tax away all income increases in excess of specified amounts. The former minister of finance spoke about this concept too. He said that he had examined the possibility of taxing away all income increases which exceed certain specified amounts. We concluded, he said, that this would result in administrative nightmares, create massive inequities but not ensure that the inflation of costs and prices would be effectively brought under control.
Why has the government changed its position? Are the provisions the Minister of Finance now refers to any different in their effect from the provisions referred to by the former minister? At that time they were called a nightmare. Is this what the present minister meant when he said that the program to be unveiled by the Prime Minister is frightening? That is the background we ought to consider as we debate the contemplated provisions of this program.
Let me be specific and talk about money. Dealing with monetary and fiscal policy the government, in its pamphlet "Attack on Inflation", says on page 4:
The fiscal stance set in the June 23, 1975 budget, together with the announced intention of the Bank of Canada to allow the money supply to expand at a rate consistent with moderate real growth and a decline in the rate of inflation, constitutes an over-all demand management policy consistent with these objectives.
In other words, the suggestion is that these actions are consistent with a responsible fiscal and monetary policy. What utter balderdash! I defy any member of the House to read that statement and tell us what it means.
We have the government's record to guide us. We know what the government's monetary stance has been. Its stance has been among the most expansive in the world. If the Prime Minister wants to go on television to tell the Canadian people the facts, he should also spell out what the government has done to the country's money system. Let him tell the people what it has done to make the printing presses spew out more and more money in this nation. Do not take my word for it, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce deals with this question in its current Commercial Letter entitled "Inflation"-in bright red letters. There is a table in the letter showing how the money supply of the major industrial countries has grown. You know, this country is not the leader in the world in many areas, but we are No. 1 now for growth of money supply in 1974.
[Mr Stevens.)
October 14, 1975

The table shows that the Canadian money supply grew by 18.9 per cent in 1974, a higher rate of growth than that shown by any nation on the list, including the United States, Austria, Belgium, France, West Germany, Italy, The Netherlands, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and Japan.
Can we take the government seriously when it says that it has launched an anti-inflation program? Can we take it seriously when we bear in mind that our money supply increased by 18.9 per cent in 1974, and that in the twelve months ending in September there was a further increase of 15 per cent? Mr. Arthur F. Burns, Chairman of the Federal Reserve Board of the United States, has said that that country would restrict its monetary growth to between 5 per cent and 7.5 per cent. On July 29, 1975, Mr. Burns appeared before the joint economic committee of Congress and said candidly that any growth in the money supply exceeding the figures just referred to would result in further inflation in his country. The United States authorities are willing to say they want to limit monetary growth to between 5 per cent and 7.5 per cent, but our government has not had the courage to tell the Canadian public its target for money growth in this country.
Despite the words spewed out about monetary restraint we know, according to the last available figures, that our money supply recently increased by $604 million. So much for limiting monetary growth. I said that that is one of the underlying pressures causing inflation in this country, and if the government were candid it would admit it.
The second underlying pressure is government spending. Here let me refer to its own figures. On page 5 of "Attack on Inflation" there is a table which shows that the federal government took 13.8 per cent of the gross national product in 1970, its take having risen from 12.9 per cent in 1965. The last figure is for 1974, which shows that the federal government took 16.1 per cent of the gross national product in that year. Governments took over 39 per cent of our gross national product in 1974, and will possibly take 40 per cent in the current year. This process has been one of the factors contributing to inflation. The Prime Minister ought to be honest with the Canadian public. This government's mismanagement has been causing inflation.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Stevens:
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has juggled cabinet positions, as well he ought to have. Consider, for example, what has happened in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Can you imagine any minister heading that department tolerating a trading deficit of $5 billion? I sincerely hope that the newly appointed Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) will, salesman that he is, introduce more imaginative programs and ensure that we sell more of our goods on world markets than is presently the case.
I have already referred to the country's lack of industrial strategy. I have touched on government regulations and their impact on business. I suggest that we, as members of parliament, must be alert in the months and years ahead, to see whether the government takes steps to reduce the bureaucracy and lessen the red tape with which business must live at present. The federal government has been
Anti-inflation
quick to regulate business still further, but has rarely cut out useless regulations. Such regulations and restrictions add to the cost of our goods and lessen industry's freedom to produce. In a free society industry's chronic problem has always been over-production, not underproducting. Recently, owing in many instances to government intervention, this had changed. Governments sanction cartels in business which, in turn, permit businesses to restrict their production and increase prices without being subject to the pressures of a free market.
The government has paid lip service in its anti-inflation program to the idea of at least reviewing such government regulations. It states that it intends to assess more carefully the cost to the private sector of many government rules and regulations in the context of their benefits to society at large. That is a welcome intention. Certainly I, for one, will watch the results of this assessment. To date, however-and I stress this-governments have continued to introduce legislation which places further controls on people and creates a greater bureaucracy to control the controls. The controls may be noble in intent, but in my opinion a lot deal with trivia, a lot are confusing, and a lot are impossible. The waste of time and energy is enormous.
I thought it interesting that the government should choose the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) to be its second spokesman on this important subject of inflation. There we have it, the king of the bureaucracy telling us how they are going to handle an anti-inflationary program. I suggest that if you add up the costs of the effects of the government's regulations in all industries and in all levels of commerce, it will prove to be a major factor in higher prices today. In fairness the government does touch on this problem in its white paper and I earnestly press the government to take action in these areas as they are spelled out in this program. The effect of such regulations is a cost that the producer or businessman cannot absorb in its entirety, so the consumer is paying for it as he has to pay taxes to keep the bureaucracy itself alive.
Touching more specifically on the program as laid down, I would point out several odd features in it. Under the definition of the cost on page 17 of the program, it deals with various ways that business can add up costs and then have a price increase, if necessary.
How is the government going to handle, for example, wholly foreign owned multi-national corporations when it deals with this question of cost? How effectively is it going to keep track of the cost of articles that may be imported from the parent company for further manufacture in Canada, and then sold? To what extent can the government guarantee to the members of this House that those articles will not be marked up in price, the cost then passed on in the form of a price increase, the net effect being the siphoning off of income to the foreign parent? It may be that that provision in the program as it is administered will end up looking like a veritable sieve.
I also note that there are many exemptions with respect to the settlements. For example, if an employer can demon-

October 14, 1975
Anti-inflation
strate that he cannot attract or hold workers at existing wages and that an increase above the guidelines is necessary, the employer will not be regarded as having breached the guidelines.
I point out these references because I think the members of this House must examine the program very carefully to ensure that there will not be inequities, that those who have a wage increase that is justifiable are not denied their increase, but on the other hand those who do not have a justifiable wage increase should be denied that wage increase. There must not only be equity, but there must be the appearance of equity in the handling of the program that we now have before us. That is why I press the government to be more specific, to give us more knowledge as to what it intends and, hopefully, leave less discretion to this anti-inflationary board when it is set up.
As my leader stated earlier, we can go along with the spirit of this anti-inflationary program. However, we emphasize that there must be much more clarification of the program than we have had to date. We are disturbed by the rather indefinite period of the program. Three years is a long time. Certainly any control program that we in this party ever contemplated would not run for that long a duration.
I know that others wish to join in this debate. I will conclude by stating that we have before us perhaps the most momentous program and the most serious deliberation that we are going to have before us in this parliament. I urge every member to take a deep interest in the program and to ensure that inequities will not occur in its administration. Second, and this I stress most strongly, let us as members of parliament keep pressing the government not only to give us rhetoric, but to back up that rhetoric with actions that will end or at least lessen inflation in this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Marshall (Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe):
subtopic: HOUSING-POSSIBILITY OF EXTENDING REHABILITATION PROGRAM AND INCREASING FUNDS AVAILABLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not see the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) in the chamber and I am not aware of the appointment of his new parliamentary secretary.
I am pleased to have the opportunity again to bring to the attention of the House the situation arising from the government's housing program which, as the result of the controls that will hopefully be implemented, is vital and timely. I hope the parliamentary secretary can convince the minister, as I have tried to do on several occasions, to increase immediately the funding under the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program. This is what I indicated to the minister in my question of July 21 last.
I repeat once again that the RRAP program is excellent. It could meet the needs of many thousands of Canadians. It could also relieve the pressure on those low and no income Canadians who own their own homes but cannot afford to maintain them. As a result their homes will continue to deteriorate and those citizens will have to join the ever-increasing numbers of those who require low rental or subsidized homes, and which the government cannot provide in the numbers needed at the present moment.
Let me give you an example, Mr. Speaker, of the tremendous value of this program to the Province of Newfoundland, a situation that is most familiar to me. The majority of Newfoundlanders in small rural communities own their
(Mr. Stevens.]
October 14, 1975

Adjournment Debate
own homes. Many of these were built without compliance to any standards simply because no standards had been established at the time. Hundreds of them are close to 50 years old and were therefore built without many of the facilities which are taken for granted today. For example, a high percentage of them are without water pipes, inside toilets, central heating and-most important-are without insulation.
This matter of insulation is one I wish to refer to the minister; it involves an issue which the minister and his colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) do not seem to want to comprehend. For some reason or other they do not want to acknowledge the waste which exists as a result of the fact that many thousands of homes, not only in Newfoundland but in every province of Canada, are improperly insulated, with the result that the cost of heating is doubled or even trebled to those occupying these sub-standard homes, particularly in the winter months.
Consider, too, Mr. Speaker, that many of the citizens occupying these homes are on welfare and that it is incumbent upon many provincial social services departments to increase the amount of assistance granted so as to cope with the added cost of home heating. It must be obvious to the minister that if more funds were made available to provinces under the RRAP program to allow for the provision of suitable electrical facilities and heating systems, and to reduce the risk run by those who live in sub-standard homes, millions of dollars and millions of gallons of heating oil would be saved, thus reducing costs which are tending, surely, to fuel the fires of inflation and increase the effect of inflation upon those who can least afford to cope with it-the poor of our country.
Apart from a statement that his department was directing attention to the matter, the only answer I received from the minister in reply to my question of July 21 was that the minister of finance of that day had eliminated the sales tax on insulation materials. I cannot accept this answer. Surely the minister knows that those to whom I refer, those who need help the most, cannot afford even to take advantage of the elimination of the sales tax by purchasing insulation materials.
The other grievance I wish to direct to the minister is that the allocation of funding for my province has been the insignificant amount of $600,000, which at best would provide relief or advantage only to some 300 homes and which would only relieve the pressures on less than 10 per cent of Newfoundland's needs.
I am sure the minister is cognizant of the needs of Canadians with regard to housing and I can only appeal to him to reassess this situation in the spirit of my presentation, to recognize realistically the facts as they exist, and to accept my suggestions which I put forward in a spirit of co-operation. I trust he will treat this as a matter of high priority, and adopt a commonsense approach when it comes to supporting a rehabilitation program and providing the funding necessary both to relieve the pressures on low income Canadians and to allow the government to cope with present housing needs, particularly since the
government is now taking steps to control the inflationary disease which so harshly affects those citizens who need the cure the most.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Robert Gauthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: HOUSING-POSSIBILITY OF EXTENDING REHABILITATION PROGRAM AND INCREASING FUNDS AVAILABLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) for giving me the first opportunity to speak in my role tonight as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. I am sure the minister appreciates the deep concern the hon. member has shown for this problem, and his remarks tonight will certainly carry the usual weight and will be studied carefully.
I should first of all refer back to the statement made on July 21, and to correct a misapprehension which is evident from the hon. member's question asked at that time. He suggested that only $7 million had been allocated for residential rehabilitation throughout Canada and that Newfoundland's share was only $600,000. These figures are correct for residential rehabilitation in rural areas, but an allocation of $39,300,000 has been made for residential rehabilitation in centres of over 2,500 people, and Newfoundland's share of that allocation is $1,300,000.
Furthermore, I am very pleased to be able to report to the House some significant progress in the area with which the hon. member is most concerned. As at September 30 of this year, in Newfoundland rehabilitation assistance applications approved and in the process of approval totalled approximately $1 million. This represents a take-up in the first nine months of this year of close to 75 per cent of the annual budget, suggesting that the program is right on target. It was the wish of the province of Newfoundland to allocate all rural rehabilitation funds to the Trout River area. Other rehabilitation loans and grants are limited to the two neighbourhood improvement areas in St. John's.
Elsewhere in Canada applications are being received at an increasing rate as other provinces proceed with the designation of municipalities and neighbourhood improvement areas. As a personal comment I would like to note that in my riding of Ottawa-Vanier I have two neighbourhood improvement areas and I am very satisfied with the way they are operating. One has been in existence for the last year, and another is just starting in Vanier.
The program is picking up steam and, as the very necessary consultations and agreements are accomplished and signed, there are indications that NIP and RRAP may enjoy a measure of success comparable to our extremely popular AHOP. It is now apparent they are meeting the need that prompted their introduction and that we can look forward to steadily increasing activity as the delivery systems are developed.
In the next few months as we give attention to the budget allocations for 1976 we will be watching closely the take-up capabilities of provinces under these two programs. Within the overall constraints we will ensure that funds are channeled from areas where they are not immediately required into those places where they can be put to the greatest use.

October 14, 1975

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Roche (Edmonton-Strathcona):
subtopic: TRANSPORT-URBAN TRANSPORTATION ASSISTANCE PROGRAM-DEFINITION OF WORDS "COMMUTER SYSTEM"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last March I asked the former Minister of Transport what progress was being made on the government's announced urban transportation assistance program, and I specifically asked the minister to ensure that the words "commuter system" would be defined to include municipal transit systems, in which case the Edmonton Northeast Rapid Transit line would qualify for assistance.
I asked that question because during the 1974 election campaign the government announced that a substantial program was forthcoming to assist urban transportation. As a matter of fact there were two or three policies enunciated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) during that compaign which drew applause throughout the country, as the people were led to believe the government was finally going to act in helping to improve urban transportation.
At that time Edmonton was beginning the construction of the Northeast Rapid Transit line, and as the third city in Canada to have a subway Edmonton was trying to find out whether it could qualify under the terms of the policy. Several months went by, and it would take far more than the time allotted here tonight to go over all the correspondence back and forth between Ottawa and Edmonton, without any definitive answer being given because the policy had not yet been so formulated that it could be put into specific terms.
Nonetheless, Edmonton having committed itself to a rapid transit system went ahead and ordered rolling stock on the ground that it was important to keep construction on schedule for the subway so that it would be in place for the Commonwealth Games of 1978.
Finally on July 30 this year the government announced some details in respect of an urban transportation assistance policy. It announced a program of $100 million to be spent over a period of five years. But what did we find when we got to the detail but the very thing I and the administration of Edmonton had feared would indeed happen, namely, that there would be excluded from the policy municipal urban transport systems? That is to say, this policy would be in force only for systems between cities, and not for systems within a city. That seemed to me to cut the heart out of the urban transportation policy that we had been lead to believe the government was interested in bringing before the country.
The policy as enunciated on July 30 said that any vehicles which had previously been ordered would be excluded from federal assistance. Edmonton of course had gone ahead and ordered its vehicles in order to keep construction on time. I suggest that the implementation of the policy announced on July 30 was discrimination against the city of Edmonton, and indeed against all of Alberta since there is no system in Alberta that will qualify for the policy as enunciated and explained on July 30.
I say to the parliamentary secretary, speaking through
him to the new minister, that if the new minister wants to
show signs that he is sincere in his determination to
represent western Canada in the government and the needs of the west, he should take a very hard look at this policy which is discriminating against Edmonton and change it so that Edmonton would qualify for $12.1 million worth of federal assistance if the rapid transit line of the city of Edmonton could be included in the policy. Edmonton has the support of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities in its endeavour to receive its just appropriation.
If the government's policy of restraint which we have been hearing a lot about in the past 24 hours is to mean anything then there must be an element of fairness in how government money is spent. I suggest that since the policy of funding would take place between 1977 and 1982, a period of five years, this would fit into any policy of restraint on government expenditures, especially if we consider the over-all effect of what public transportation does in this country in cutting down automobile costs in heavily urbanized centres.
Indeed we know that for every $1 spent on cars in urban centres less than five cents is spent on public transportation. That is a shame in a society which is now beginning to pride itself on energy conservation, and indeed at a time when the government is spending enormous sums of money on advertising programs to convince Canadians that we must save energy in respect of heating and mobile costs. Therefore I suggest that at the tri-level meetings which are continuing in this country, with governments trying to get together, and in which I myself participated on September 29 in Edmonton, if there is to be a spirit of trust and mutual confidence then we must expect that the government will be honest with the people of Alberta and say that when it announced the policy in an election campaign it intended to deliver on it over a period in harmony with a policy of restraint and of energy conservation. The government should be honest with the people and not exclude us. So, for energy saving and a proper energy policy for the west, and indeed for the credibility of the new Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), to whom I wish success, I say it is absolutely imperative that he re-assess that policy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-URBAN TRANSPORTATION ASSISTANCE PROGRAM-DEFINITION OF WORDS "COMMUTER SYSTEM"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say at the beginning that I am very pleased at this first opportunity which I have to participate in the debate in the House as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, and I am glad to do so in response to the remarks of a fellow westerner. I took very careful note of the hon. member's comments with respect to what he perceives quite rightly to be the deep concern of the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) for the position of western Canada in Confederation and his aspirations in that regard. I can assure the hon. member that those aspirations are shared by many of us in all parts of the House.
As the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) is undoubtedly aware, and indeed as he has just pointed out quite correctly, the problem of traffic congestion and its related evils such as automobile accidents, pollution, and urban sprawl, have become prevalent within our urban areas. A promising way to alleviate these prob-

October 14, 1975

lems is to increase the use of urban commuter and transit services in order to reduce the number of cars on the road.
Canadian municipalities have improved public transportation services in recent years with financial aid from provincial governments; the announcement of the federal intention last year to provide further capital assistance for urban transportation was warmly received by provincial and municipal spokesmen, and the media.
The former minister of transport, and the present Minister responsible for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) announced on July 30, 1975, a federal government capital assistance program for urban transportation. This program deals specifically with assistance for urban commuter services and provides for up to 75 per cent of the cost of new vehicles for such services in the form of grants, and a further 25 per cent in loans. This program will provide technical and planning assistance to municipalities, but particularly to those smaller ones which may have a need. As the Minister of State for Urban Affairs stated earlier,
Adjournment Debate
there has never been conflict between officials of the Ministry of Transport and those of the Department of State for Urban Affairs, and the announced program is the result of close collaboration between officials of the two Ministries. Furthermore, these two ministries are working very closely together in an examination of further initiatives that the federal government might take in the future in the area of urban transportation.
As the hon. member may know, the present Minister of Transport after assuming the transport portfolio did have occasion to meet briefly in Ottawa recently with His Worship Mayor Horawlec of Edmonton, and he indicated to the mayor at that time that he would re-examine the question of federal government support for the Edmonton rapid transit system.
